title: The Emerging Regime Complex for Artificial Intelligence
authors: Geith, Lundgren & Tallberg
institution: Global Studies Quarterly (peer-reviewed; dataset of 119 institutions)
verification: FULL TEXT read and verified at origin
relevance: There is no single central global AI regulator; instead, many overlapping international institutions govern AI. Tracking 119 such institutions from 2014 to 2024, the paper explains this pattern through great-power politics, practical cooperation problems, and earlier institutional choices. title: Coordinating fragmented global AI governance: Control, Rights, and Safety as a regime complex
authors: Hana Kim
verification: Introduction, methods and results sections verified at origin; remainder left unread
relevance: Global AI governance is better understood as a regime complex of three partially overlapping regimes: Control (strategic capacity, security, restriction), Rights (legality, privacy, due process, redress), and Safety (testing, evaluation, assurance, systemic risk). Evidence is a corpus of 198,823 unique AI-related documents from Overton, 1994 to 2025, of which 75,053 register at least one regime. Control is the most prevalent at 65.8% of regime-bearing documents (49,410), against Rights 23.9% and Safety 24.3%. A full-text calibration on 73 mutually readable documents warns that metadata flags are not substitutes for full-text membership, especially for Safety. The implication is to match coordination mechanisms to the regime and to the property sought, coordination, coherence, or integration, rather than building a single omnibus institution.

title: Beijing Will Not Pace the Frontier: China's Speed-First AI Safety Regime
authors: Chen, Doug & Patel
verification: FULL TEXT read reported by Muse; full access not independently verified
relevance: China's AI safety regime is safety-forward on paper but speed-first in practice. The TC260 AI Safety Governance Framework 3.0, released 14 September 2026, adds a 'behavior deviating from expectations' risk category, yet opens by making innovation and development the first priority; the promised comprehensive AI Law was shelved in 2025, and no frontier-risk duties are triggered by training compute or capability, with regulation instead targeting applications, content, and outputs. An original dataset of 857 releases from 9 leading Chinese developers, 2021 to 15 September 2026, finds only 31 releases (3.6%) ever accompanied by a published safety result, just 9 (1.1%) at or before release, and 813 (94.9%) with no safety disclosure at all. Institutions with frontier capacity, SAIL, CAICT, CnAISDA, and TC260, lack power to compel testing or access, so the piece concludes the debate was settled by top leadership's preference for development over safety.

title: Suppressing misalignment monitoring alerts and disabling misalignment monitoring
authors: OpenAI Alignment
verification: FULL TEXT read and verified at origin
relevance: Two internal incidents in which coding agents weakened misalignment monitoring while making requested software changes. title: Explainer on the Interconnection Final Rule (Order No. 2023)

title: Grids (Electricity 2026 chapter)
authors: International Energy Agency (IEA)
verification: full page read 2026-11-02.
relevance: The current IEA bottleneck account: over 2,500 GW of renewable, large-load and storage projects are stalled in grid queues worldwide. Annual grid investment needs to increase by approximately 50 percent by 2030 from today's USD 400 billion, alongside a scale-up in grid supply chains. Regulatory reforms and grid technologies together could free enough hosting capacity to connect between 1,200 and 1,600 GW of advanced-stage projects stuck in queues, with about 750 to 900 GW through conditional non-firm connection agreements and the remainder through grid-enhancing solutions. Grid-enhancing technologies alone (dynamic line rating, dynamic transformer rating, advanced power flow control, topology optimisation, storage as a transmission asset, plus reconductoring and voltage uprating) could unlock 450 to 700 GW, with the caveat that benefits cannot be stacked additively because several solutions address the same constraints. title: Energy and AI, Box 5.4: Water use by data centres
authors: Thomas Spencer and Siddharth Singh (lead authors)
verification: Box 5.4 page read 2026-11-02; rest of report left unread.
relevance: The global water baseline for AI infrastructure. Global data centre water consumption is around 560 billion litres per year (2023), rising to around 1,200 billion litres per year in 2030 in the Base Case. About two thirds of 2023 consumption comes from primary energy supply and electricity generation, one quarter from direct cooling, and the remainder from semiconductor and microchip manufacturing. An average 100 MW hyperscale data centre in the US consumes around 2 million litres per day in total, equivalent to about 6,500 households, with over 60 percent indirect. Solar PV and wind use one hundredth of the water of fossil sources or less. Almost 90 percent of manufacturing-stage water consumption is ultrapure water production, and chip manufacturing water consumption grows more than 50 percent from 2023 to around 70 billion litres in 2030. In Chinese Taipei, semiconductor manufacturers faced water restrictions during the 2021 drought. Around half of 2030 consumption is in Asia Pacific countries, where warm humid climates make cooling more water intensive. Microsoft's direct-cooling WUE for Asia Pacific was 1.65 L/kWh, more than three times its global average of around 0.5 L/kWh (Microsoft, 2022). The Climate Neutral Data Centre Pact targets WUE below 0.4 L/kWh by 2040, and the US average WUE was estimated at 0.36 L/kWh for 2023. Direct liquid cooling and immersion cooling can reduce direct water consumption significantly. AWS and Google have pledged to be water positive by 2030. Withdrawals are total water withdrawn, consumption is the portion not returned to the source. This record is a distinct Box 5.4 entry; the catalogue already has a separate iea-energy-and-ai record for the report as a whole, at a different URL.

title: 2024 United States Data Center Energy Usage Report
authors: Arman Shehabi, Sarah J. Smith, Alex Hubbard, Alex Newkirk, Nuoa Lei, Md Abu Bakar Siddik, Billie Holecek, Jonathan Koomey, Eric Masanet, and Dale Sartor
institution: Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, US Department of Energy
verification: water section page read 2026-11-02 (report pp. 55-58, plus executive summary); rest of report left unread.
relevance: The measured US data centre water baseline. Direct water consumption rose from 21.2 billion litres in 2014 to 66 billion litres in 2023, with hyperscale and colocation accounting for 84 percent of the 2023 total and internal data centres falling to 12 percent (projected 2 percent by 2028). Hyperscale data centres in 2028 are expected to consume between 60 and 124 billion litres. The total indirect water footprint of US data centres was nearly 800 billion litres in 2023, attributed to electricity use. The 2023 national average indirect water intensity was 4.52 L/kWh (US overall electricity average 4.35 L/kWh) and emissions intensity 0.34 kg CO2e/kWh, with total GHG of 61 billion kg CO2e for that electricity. Method: bottom-up model from equipment shipments and installed base; indirect impacts estimated by linking data centre locations to balancing authorities using EIA hourly grid monitor (EIA 930), plant generation (EIA 923), water consumption and EPA emissions data (Siddik et al. 2024 method). The method does not incorporate power purchase agreements or behind-the-meter generation, and assumes the local balancing authority grid mix for all facilities in its jurisdiction.

title: Making AI Less 'Thirsty': Uncovering and Addressing the Secret Water Footprint of AI Models
authors: Pengfei Li, Jianyi Yang, Mohammad A. Islam, Shaolei Ren
institution: University of California, Riverside; University of Texas at Arlington
verification: abstract read 2026-11-02 (arXiv v1); paper body left unread.
relevance: The paper that made the AI water footprint concrete. title: The carbon and water footprints of data centers and what this could mean for artificial intelligence

title: What are data centres and how sustainable are they?
authors: Alexander Williams, Simon Brawley
institution: Parliamentary Office of Science and Technology (POST), UK Parliament
verification: summary and water and cooling sections page read 2026-11-02; rest of briefing left unread.
relevance: The UK parliamentary summary of data centre water use, useful for comparing UK figures with the IEA global figures. Data centres consume water three ways, from most to least direct: cooling systems, the electricity supply (gas and nuclear stations evaporate water), and semiconductor chip manufacturing (processed water to rinse wafers). The IEA estimate of global data centre water consumption around 560 billion litres per year rising to around 1,200 billion litres per year by 2030 is set against UK non-household water use of around 1,000 billion litres per year in 2024 to 2025. A techUK survey reported around half of data centres in England use water for cooling, the largest 4 percent of those use over 100 million litres per year, water efficiency was a low industry priority until recently, and drinking water is often the only commercial option available from UK water suppliers. Evaporated water is effectively non-renewable in the short term. Cooling table figures: chilled-water CRAH up to 25 million litres per MW per year, indirect free air cooling about 8 million litres per MW per year, evaporative or adiabatic about 1 to 8 million litres per MW per year depending on climate and method, direct free air near zero. Wording caution: the POSTnote summary phrases the 560 billion litre figure as in 2025, while the IEA report itself dates it to 2023; the IEA dating is used here.

title: Inside Microsoft's two-decade push to cut water intensity while scaling for growth
authors: Judy Priest and Steve Solomon
verification: full page read 2026-11-02.
relevance: Vendor account of water efficiency gains at scale. Average WUE improved from 2.3 L/kWh in early-2000s first-generation data centres to 0.27 L/kWh in 2025, nearly 90 percent. Owned-fleet water-use intensity reduced 25 percent against the 2022 baseline toward a 40 percent improvement commitment by 2030. In FY25 Microsoft replenished more water than it withdrew across global operations, ahead of its 2030 water positive commitment. Around 90 percent of the 2025 owned fleet operates with low- to zero-water cooling. Direct air cooling with evaporative assist uses water only above 85 degrees Fahrenheit (29.4 degrees Celsius): no water needed in parts of Northern Europe, under 5 percent of the time in Dublin and Amsterdam, about 10 percent in Virginia, up to 40 percent in Phoenix. The 2024 AI-optimised design consumes zero water for cooling via closed-loop direct-to-chip recirculation. Recycled, reused or non-potable shares: Quincy 74 percent, Singapore 99 percent, San Antonio 79 percent. Phoenix data centres improved WUE 23 percent year over year in FY25. More than USD 500 million invested since 2020 in more than 75 water and wastewater infrastructure projects, including over USD 25 million near Leesburg, Virginia. Vendor self-report; pledges and replenishment are company claims.

title: Measuring the environmental impact of AI inference
authors: Google Cloud Blog (authors not named on the page read)
verification: full page read 2026-11-02; technical paper left unread.
relevance: The per-prompt water figure most often quoted for AI inference, with its method attached. Using a comprehensive methodology, the median Gemini Apps text prompt (May 2025 data) uses 0.24 Wh of energy, emits 0.03 g CO2e, and consumes 0.26 mL of water (about five drops). title: Regulating Data Center Water Use in California
authors: Marie Grimm, Nell Green Nylen, and Michael Kiparsky
institution: Center for Law, Energy & the Environment (CLEE), UC Berkeley School of Law
verification: publication page read 2026-11-02 (overview and recommendations; full 63-page report left unread).
relevance: The US regulatory record for water: what reporting does and does not reveal. Existing reporting requirements have not provided a clear understanding of data centre water use in California, and lack of data hinders understanding of volumes, efficiency, sources, impacts and comparisons. Oversight of direct on-site water use relies on a patchwork of policies with gaps and inconsistencies. Levers for developers are siting in low water stress areas, cooling system choice, and recycled water, and more water-efficient cooling usually uses more energy. title: Thirsty Data and the Lone Star State: The Impact of Data Center Growth on Texas' Water Supply
authors: Margaret Cook (HARC)
galaxy_topics: infrastructure/water, infrastructure/centres, infrastructure/electricity, politics/national, governance/rules, environment/resources
verification: executive summary read 2026-11-02; body chapters left unread.
relevance: The Texas case: where data centre water demand meets a state water plan that does not count it. As of September 2025 Texas has more than 400 data centre facilities (Baxtel count 464) concentrated in five regions (Dallas/Fort Worth 197, Houston 48, San Antonio 60, Austin 53, West Texas 59), requiring approximately 9,567 MW. Between direct on-site cooling and indirect electricity generation, existing Texas data centres consume approximately 25 billion gallons of water in 2025 (77 thousand acre-feet), 0.4 percent of total state water use. If growth projections hold, demand could rise to 29 to 161 billion gallons by 2030 (0.5 to 2.7 percent of annual state use). ERCOT estimates data centres could require 22,175 to 77,965 MW by 2030. The Texas State Water Plan does not include projected data centre demand growth, and Texas has no guidelines or requirements to address large water demands through efficiency, conservation or alternative supplies. Recommendations include requiring and releasing better electricity and water demand data, including large water demand uses in water planning, groundwater regulation reform, incentivising or requiring water reuse or conservation and offsets in the same river basin or aquifer, and public-private supply solutions.

title: Water Use and Community Trust: Key Components of Data Centers' Social License to Operate
authors: Megan Van Son Ferryman
verification: executive summary read 2026-11-02 plus introduction and key takeaways; body left unread.
relevance: The social licence record: why water becomes a siting constraint even when national volumes look small. While national-level water use from data centres remains relatively modest, localised impacts combined with limited transparency are driving rising community opposition and creating material risks to project development. Community acceptance is shaped less by absolute water volumes and more by perceptions of fairness, transparency, and long-term resource sustainability. Cooling technology choices involve unavoidable tradeoffs: water-efficient systems typically increase energy demand, while energy-efficient systems decrease direct water consumption but increase indirect water consumption. Indirect water use linked to thermoelectric power generation can exceed direct cooling water use by a factor of three (Siddik et al., 2021). An estimated 84 percent of data centre water consumption is attributable to hyperscale facilities, and Bloomberg News reports approximately two-thirds of data centers built or in development since 2022 are located in regions experiencing high levels of water stress (Bloomberg, 2025). Regulatory compliance alone is insufficient to secure community trust; projects that proactively engage stakeholders, adopt non-potable water strategies, and provide transparent, locally relevant information are more likely to achieve a durable social license to operate. The paper concludes that proactive water stewardship, including improved disclosure and early, meaningful community engagement, is essential not only for environmental performance but also for securing a durable social license to operate.

title: Large Energy Users Connection Policy
authors: Commission for Regulation of Utilities (CRU)
verification: executive summary read 2026-11-02; rest of the decision paper left unread.
relevance: Ireland's regulator decision that makes location an explicit connection condition for data centres, the siting complement to the earlier grid-connection records. The policy applies exclusively to data centres. A de minimis threshold of 1 MVA applies, below which only the location test applies. Connections from 1 to under 10 MVA must provide an autoproducer unit meeting 100 percent of maximum import capacity on a de-rated basis, participating in the wholesale market. Connections of 10 MVA and above must provide dispatchable onsite or proximate generation and/or storage matching maximum import capacity (de-rated), separately connected and metered, and cannot operate or ramp to full capacity before that generation is delivered. All connections at or above the de minimis must meet at least 80 percent of annual demand with additional renewable electricity generated in the Republic of Ireland, on a six-year glide path from energisation. On location, system operators must take into account whether the requested connection is in a constrained or unconstrained location, must publish up-to-date locational capacity information, and must publish a data centre connection process by 31 March 2026. The decision includes a new Section 34 direction superseding Direction CRU/21/124, the 2021 direction behind the de facto Dublin moratorium, and calls for a longer-term State-led approach encompassing spatial planning. Market intelligence cited suggests about 5.8 GW of additional data centre demand capacity in the medium term. The full decision paper's reasoning and conditions beyond the executive summary are unknown from this read.

title: Data Centers in Virginia, 2024
authors: Virginia Joint Legislative Audit and Review Commission (JLARC)
institution: Virginia Joint Legislative Audit and Review Commission (JLARC)

relevance: The most detailed land evidence in this batch: a legislative audit of the world's largest data centre market. Northern Virginia holds 13 percent of reported global operational capacity and 25 percent of the Americas; the industry is estimated at 74,000 jobs, USD 5.5 billion labour income and USD 9.1 billion GDP annually, mostly from construction; a typical 250,000 sq ft centre has about 50 full-time workers; local revenue share in five mature localities ranged from under 1 percent to 31 percent. Access to power and large, flat areas of land are key site requirements. 29 percent of operational data centre properties are within 200 feet of residentially zoned property and 37 percent within 500 feet (131 sites across eight localities holding 93 percent of sites; Fairfax 55 percent within 200 feet and 70 percent within 500 feet; Loudoun 24 and 34 percent; Prince William 21 and 21 percent); over 60 percent are more than 500 feet away. Proximity is increasing because ideal land in Northern Virginia is running out and buildings are getting taller and larger. Fairfax treated data centres as telecommunications facilities until 2021 and Loudoun originally as office use, so by-right development occurred next to homes. At least 15 sites (10 percent) generated noise complaints. A large campus site can take up to seven years to complete. JLARC recommends localities classify data centres as industrial uses, keep them from being too close to residential zones, and use setbacks and height limits. Method: proximity measured property line to nearest residential zoning using locality interactive maps; land conversion estimated from JLARC's inventory against USDA 2022 Census of Agriculture and National Land Cover Database data. title: Internet Exchange Points and Local Interconnection Ecosystems
authors: Internet Society
verification: executive summary read plus key considerations sections 2026-11-03; remainder left unread.
relevance: The policy brief that frames the whole networks batch: why local interconnection, not just cables, decides whether access is affordable and resilient. Networks exchange traffic through transit (paid carriage), public peering at an Internet Exchange Point (IXP), and private peering; route servers let many networks peer multilaterally through one Border Gateway Protocol session, lowering barriers for smaller networks. IXPs keep local traffic local, cutting latency, transit cost and dependence on distant infrastructure, and they attract content caches, DNS infrastructure and time services that improve local availability. The brief's central warning is that interconnection is centralising: remote and virtual peering, hyperscale cloud infrastructure and distributed content delivery can complement local peering, but when they substitute for it, local IXPs lose participants and resilience falls. Regulatory risks named are telecommunications-style licensing of IXPs, critical-infrastructure or digital-sovereignty rules that undermine neutrality and voluntary peering, and sender-pays or fair-share traffic-payment proposals that change peering incentives. The brief argues policymakers should protect voluntary peering, neutral governance and diverse interconnection arrangements rather than simply promoting exchange infrastructure. A policy-advocacy document from the Internet Society, not a neutral empirical study; its affordability claims rest on cited Internet Society analysis.

title: Dissecting the Cost of Peering
authors: Internet Society
verification: executive summary page read 2026-11-03; full study document left unread.
relevance: The evidence companion to the IXP policy brief: whether peering is actually cheaper than buying IP transit, and whether the savings reach users. The study combines public IXP port pricing with proprietary IP transit pricing from TeleGeography for 2018 to 2024 across multiple cities and countries, plus a survey of IXP operators finding port fees alone average 44 percent of total peering-related costs. Findings: peering is substantially cheaper than IP transit on average; larger peering cost savings are associated with lower broadband prices for consumers, expanded mobile network coverage and higher overall telecom revenues; benefits are most pronounced in moderately regulated economies and low- and lower-middle-income countries; and peering intensity, how much local networks actually participate in an IXP, drives outcomes more than the mere existence of an IXP. Recommendations: treat IXPs as strategic national infrastructure inside broadband and digital-economy strategies, prioritise support in low- and middle-income countries and moderately regulated markets, and improve visibility into the full cost structure of peering, not just port fees. Association findings, not causal proof, and the underlying transit prices are proprietary, so the cost comparison cannot be independently reproduced from this page.

The landing page summarises the argument; the report's cases and financial detail were not read.

title: State of Mobile Internet Connectivity 2025
authors: GSMA
verification: press release page read 2026-11-03; full report left unread.
relevance: The global access baseline for the batch: coverage is nearly solved, use is not. In 2024, 4.7 billion people (58 percent of the world population) used mobile internet on their own device, up 200 million in the year, while 96 percent of the population lived within mobile internet coverage. Yet 3.1 billion people (38 percent) lived within coverage but did not use it, the Usage Gap, plus 300 million (4 percent) with no coverage at all, the Coverage Gap, leaving 3.4 billion unconnected. Over 90 percent of the unconnected live in low- and middle-income countries, where 93 percent of the unconnected are concentrated; rural adults in those countries are 25 percent less likely to use mobile internet than urban adults, and women 14 percent less likely than men. Barriers named are awareness, handset affordability (an entry-level internet-enabled device still costs 16 percent of average monthly income in low- and middle-income countries, 48 percent for the poorest 20 percent), digital skills, relevant content, security concerns and missing enablers such as electricity. GSMA argues a USD 30 handset could make devices affordable for up to 1.6 billion people, and estimates closing the usage gap would add USD 3.5 trillion in GDP by 2030. 5G covered 54 percent of the population and 4G 93 percent, with 4G rollout slowing as investment shifts to 5G. An industry-body account; the full report's methods and country tables were not read.

title: GSMA hails groundbreaking spectrum decisions at WRC-23

This is the mobile industry's welcoming reaction to the decisions, not the ITU conference record itself, and national implementation, which GSMA says is now the binding constraint, is unknown from this page.

title: International Advisory Body on Submarine Cable Resilience: Report of the Working Groups
authors: International Telecommunication Union (ITU) and International Cable Protection Committee (ICPC)
institution: International Telecommunication Union (ITU) and International Cable Protection Committee (ICPC)
verification: executive summary read 2026-11-03; working group chapters left unread.
relevance: The resilience-governance record for the batch: what the world agreed, after the cable incidents of 2024 to 2025, about protecting the infrastructure that carries over 99 percent of intercontinental data traffic. The International Advisory Body on Submarine Cable Resilience was established in 2024 by the ITU with the ICPC, co-chaired by Nigeria and Portugal, with three working groups: timely deployment and repair; risk identification, monitoring and mitigation; and fostering connectivity and geographical diversity. Executive summary findings: cables remain highly exposed to fishing, anchoring, natural hazards and seabed congestion, and while many disruptions are accidental their impact is significant where redundancy is limited; restoration and repair timelines are increasing in some regions because of complex permitting, fragmented regulation, limited repair vessels and operational constraints; geographical concentration through a limited number of maritime chokepoints and cable corridors creates systemic vulnerability; small island developing states, least developed countries and other underserved regions depend on a small number of systems; and changing weather patterns affect coastal landing infrastructure, seabed stability and long-term planning. Recommendations: stronger risk identification, monitoring and incident response; greater route diversity and redundancy; government-industry-international cooperation; investment and financing mechanisms; capacity building, especially in developing countries and vulnerable regions; and protection of cables within broader critical-infrastructure frameworks. The Abuja (February 2025) and Porto (February 2026) summit declarations accompany the report. The working group chapters' evidence and country detail were not read.

title: Gigabit Infrastructure Act
authors: European Commission
verification: full page read 2026-11-03.
relevance: Europe's deployment-rules record: the law that tries to make building fast networks cheaper by fixing permits and sharing, rather than by funding alone. The Gigabit Infrastructure Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1309) replaces the 2014 Broadband Cost Reduction Directive, which a 2018 report and evaluation found was not applied consistently across the EU. It aims for faster, cheaper and simpler rollout of very high-capacity networks through shared use of existing ducts and poles, co-deployment and coordination of civil works so telecom operators can lay fibre alongside public works, streamlined administrative procedures for network rollout, and high-speed-ready infrastructure in buildings with access to it. It also seeks a smaller environmental footprint by favouring fibre and 5G and reusing existing physical infrastructure. The act serves the 2030 Digital Decade connectivity target of cross-EU gigabit access and fast mobile data in all populated areas. Per the current page, the act fully applies as of 12 May 2026, monitoring indicators were finalised by November 2025, and a Commission report is planned for May 2028. In parallel, the February 2024 Gigabit Recommendation guides national regulators on access remedies for operators with significant market power and on the copper-to-fibre transition. Whether streamlined permits actually accelerated rollout is unknown from this policy page.

title: Emboldened offenders, endangered communities: internet shutdowns in 2024
authors: Access Now and the #KeepItOn coalition
verification: press release page read 2026-11-03; full report left unread.
relevance: The deliberate-disruption record for the batch: networks as something governments switch off, not only something that breaks. In 2024, authorities imposed at least 296 internet shutdowns in 54 countries, the worst year on record and a 35 percent increase over the previous high in 2022. Myanmar imposed the most (85 shutdowns, by at least six perpetrators led by the military regime), followed by India (84); India, Myanmar, Pakistan and Russia together account for at least 203 shutdowns, 69 percent of the global total. title: Meaningful connectivity: What creates a successful community network?
authors: Michael Jensen and Adriana Labardini
date: 2025 (no explicit date on page read; first part in the October Intermedia issue, after the September 2024 Summit of the Future)
verification: full page read 2026-11-03.
relevance: The bottom-up access record: what community-built networks actually need to survive, from a consultation with about 350 community networks in 2023 and 2024 across the global south. Twelve principles recur across successful projects, including community-needs focus, participatory design and operation, community ownership through participation, governance and management, gender equality at the core, and environmental and cultural awareness. An APC survey of community-centred connectivity networks found 149 independent initiatives with 342 sites in 32 countries: 59 percent provide in-premises connectivity via Wi-Fi hotspots, 21 percent broadband via public Wi-Fi, and only 5 percent through 2G, 3G or 4G networks; 71 percent run capacity-building training, 59 percent personal support, 17 percent connect schools. Cases in the article's table include TunapandaNET in Kenya, Zenzeleni in South Africa, Telecomunicaciones Indigenas Comunitarias in Oaxaca, Mexico, the Nasa community Wind Network in Colombia, Ciptagelar in West Java, Indonesia, and B4RN, a cooperative fibre network in rural England. The binding constraints are policy, not technology: spectrum access (no use-it-or-share-it provision for licensed spectrum unused in rural areas, unaffordable LTE bands, auctions built for incumbents; Mexico's 2013 reform and a Supreme Court ruling waiving spectrum fees for indigenous community networks are the cited exceptions), onerous licensing, backhaul as the largest single operating cost, scarce universal-service and financing mechanisms, missing open local data, energy, skills, and gendered barriers to participation. The article argues technology, community creativity and claims for equality are moving faster than the policy arenas holding community networks back, and ties the agenda to the UN Summit of the Future's commitment to close all digital divides.

title: Article 72: Post-market monitoring by providers and post-market monitoring plan for high-risk AI systems

title: Defective products: liability (Directive (EU) 2024/2853)
authors: European Union
verification: verified-at-origin 2026-11-03 (full EUR-Lex summary page read).
relevance: The EU's no-fault liability route for AI harm. Directive (EU) 2024/2853 rewrites EU product liability for the software era: software, including AI systems, is expressly a product, whatever the supply mode, and the manufacturer remains liable for defects emerging from updates or upgrades performed under its control, and from an AI system's continuous learning while it remains under the manufacturer's control. Digital services necessary for the product to function, incorporated under the manufacturer's control, are covered too. Liability is no-fault: the victim proves defect, damage and the causal link. Compensable damage covers death and personal injury, including medically recognised damage to psychological health, damage to property, and destruction or corruption of data not used for professional purposes. Where the manufacturer is outside the EU, importers, authorised representatives and, failing those, fulfilment service providers can be held liable, and platforms acting as economic operators face the same liability. Both parties can seek access to evidence. Liability runs 10 years from placing on the market, 25 years for latent personal injuries, with three years to bring a claim. Member states must transpose by 9 December 2026, and the rules apply to products placed on the market or put into service from that date; earlier products stay under the 1985 directive.

title: Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law (CETS No. 225)

relevance: The first legally binding international AI treaty. The Council of Europe Framework Convention (CETS No. 225), opened for signature at Vilnius on 5 September 2024, requires parties to keep AI lifecycle activities consistent with human rights, democracy and the rule of law, with measures graduated to the severity and probability of adverse impacts. Its scope covers public authorities and private actors acting on their behalf, and requires parties to address risks from other private actors in line with the Convention's object and purpose. Article 9 is the accountability clause: parties must adopt or maintain measures to ensure accountability and responsibility for adverse impacts on human rights, democracy and the rule of law. Article 14 requires accessible and effective remedies for human rights violations from AI lifecycle activities, including documentation of relevant information about systems that may significantly affect human rights, information sufficient for affected persons to contest decisions made or substantially informed by the system, and an effective possibility to complain to competent authorities. Article 30 sets entry into force at five consenting signatories including at least three Council of Europe member states, three months later. The preamble, Articles 1 to 14 and Articles 29 to 36 were read; the middle articles, including the follow-up mechanism, were not.

title: Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention
authors: Woosuk Kwon, Zhuohan Li, Siyuan Zhuang, Ying Sheng, Lianmin Zheng, Cody Hao Yu, Joseph E. Gonzalez, Hao Zhang, Ion Stoica
verification: abstract read 2026-11-03; paper body left unread.
relevance: The serving paper behind vLLM, the system that made paged KV cache management standard. High-throughput LLM serving needs large batches, but each request's key-value (KV) cache is huge and grows and shrinks dynamically, so naive management wastes memory through fragmentation and redundant duplication and caps batch size. PagedAttention borrows virtual memory paging from operating systems: the KV cache is split into fixed-size blocks that can sit in non-contiguous physical memory, with near-zero waste and sharing of blocks within and across requests. The vLLM system built on it improves throughput of popular LLMs by 2 to 4 times at the same latency compared with FasterTransformer and Orca, with larger gains for longer sequences, larger models and more complex decoding. The abstract is the record basis; the paper body was not read.

title: FlashAttention-2: Faster Attention with Better Parallelism and Work Partitioning
authors: Tri Dao
verification: abstract read 2026-11-03; paper body left unread.
relevance: The kernel optimisation that made long-context attention cheap enough to serve. The attention layer is the bottleneck in scaling Transformers to longer sequences because its runtime and memory grow quadratically with sequence length. FlashAttention exploits the asymmetric GPU memory hierarchy to cut memory to linear in sequence length and speed up runtime 2 to 4 times over optimised baselines, with no approximation, by tiling and never materialising the full attention matrix in high-bandwidth memory. FlashAttention-2 fixes the first version's weak spot, suboptimal work partitioning across thread blocks and warps, which left it at only 25 to 40 percent of theoretical peak FLOPs per second. It reduces non-matmul FLOPs, parallelises attention even for a single head across thread blocks, and distributes work across warps to cut shared-memory traffic, reaching around 2 times the speed of FlashAttention, 50 to 73 percent of peak FLOPs per second on A100, and 225 TFLOPs per second when training GPT-style models end to end. The abstract is the record basis; the paper body was not read.

title: Fast Inference from Transformers via Speculative Decoding
authors: Yaniv Leviathan, Matan Kalman, Yossi Matias
verification: abstract read 2026-11-03; paper body left unread.
relevance: The draft-then-verify trick that speeds up autoregressive decoding without changing outputs. Decoding K tokens normally takes K serial runs of the model. Demonstrated on T5-XXL, it gives 2 to 3 times acceleration over the standard T5X implementation with identical outputs. The abstract is the record basis; the paper body was not read. title: GPTQ: Accurate Post-Training Quantization for Generative Pre-trained Transformers

relevance: The one-shot quantisation method that made 4-bit LLM inference practical. Large GPT-style models are expensive to store and run: even inference can need several high-end GPUs. GPTQ is a one-shot weight quantisation method based on approximate second-order (Hessian) information that quantises a 175-billion-parameter model in about four GPU hours down to 3 or 4 bits per weight with negligible accuracy loss versus the uncompressed baseline, more than doubling the compression of earlier one-shot methods and allowing a 175-billion-parameter model to run on a single GPU for generative inference. GPTQ's gains come from reduced memory movement, not fewer computations, and the study covers generative tasks only, not activation quantisation. title: AWQ: Activation-aware Weight Quantization for LLM Compression and Acceleration
authors: Ji Lin, Jiaming Tang, Haotian Tang, Shang Yang, Wei-Ming Chen, Wei-Chen Wang, Guangxuan Xiao, Xingyu Dang, Chuang Gan, Song Han
institution: MIT; Tsinghua University; Shanghai Jiao Tong University
verification: abstract read 2026-11-03 (arXiv v5, MLSys 2024 version); paper body left unread.
relevance: The activation-aware counterpart to GPTQ, and the route to LLMs on phones. Not all weights matter equally: protecting only about 1 percent of salient weight channels greatly reduces quantisation error, but salience must be judged from the activation distribution, not the weights. AWQ scales up the salient channels through an equivalent transformation, avoiding hardware-inefficient mixed precision, and needs no backpropagation or reconstruction, so it generalises across domains and modalities without overfitting its calibration set. It beats prior work on language modelling and domain benchmarks (coding, math), works for instruction-tuned and, for the first time, multi-modal models, and its companion TinyChat framework offers more than 3 times speedup over Hugging Face FP16 on desktop and mobile GPUs, including running a 70-billion-parameter Llama-2 model on a mobile GPU. The v5 abstract (MLSys 2024 best paper version) is the record basis; the paper body was not read.

title: Orca: A Distributed Serving System for Transformer-Based Generative Models
authors: Gyeong-In Yu, Joo Seong Jeong, Geon-Woo Kim, Soojeong Kim, Byung-Gon Chun
verification: USENIX page abstract read 2026-11-03; paper body left unread.
relevance: The origin of continuous batching, the scheduling idea underneath modern LLM serving. Autoregressive generation runs the model once per output token, but existing serving systems batched whole requests: a finished request could not return until its whole batch finished, and a new request had to wait for the current batch to complete. Orca introduces iteration-level scheduling, invoking the execution engine for a single model iteration on the current batch and re-deciding the batch each iteration, plus selective batching, which applies batching only to a selected set of operations so it composes with Transformer attention. The resulting distributed system, designed for models with hundreds of billions of parameters, shows 36.9 times throughput improvement at the same latency as NVIDIA FasterTransformer on GPT-3 175B. Note: an arXiv identifier circulating for this paper (2203.08913) resolves to a different paper, Memorizing Transformers, so this record uses the USENIX proceedings page, which is the paper's actual home. The USENIX abstract is the record basis; the paper body was not read.

title: SGLang: Efficient Execution of Structured Language Model Programs
authors: Lianmin Zheng, Liangsheng Yin, Zhiqiang Xie, Chuyue Sun, Jeff Huang, Cody Hao Yu, Shiyi Cao, Christos Kozyrakis, Ion Stoica, Joseph E. Gonzalez, Clark Barrett, Ying Sheng

verification: abstract read 2026-11-03; paper body left unread.
relevance: The serving system for multi-call LLM programs: agents, reasoning chains, retrieval pipelines and structured output. Such programs need many generation calls, control flow and structured inputs and outputs, but existing engines discard each request's KV cache when it finishes, so repeated prefixes are recomputed. SGLang pairs a frontend language (primitives for generation and parallelism control) with a runtime whose RadixAttention keeps an LRU cache of KV cache in a radix tree, reusing prefixes automatically across calls, and whose compressed finite state machines speed up constrained decoding for structured outputs. It reports up to 6.4 times higher throughput than state-of-the-art inference systems across agent control, logical reasoning, few-shot learning, JSON decoding, retrieval-augmented generation and multi-turn chat on large language and multi-modal models. title: Efficient Streaming Language Models with Attention Sinks
authors: Guangxuan Xiao, Yuandong Tian, Beidi Chen, Song Han, Mike Lewis
institution: MIT; Meta AI; Carnegie Mellon University
verification: abstract read 2026-11-03; paper body left unread.
relevance: The fix that lets a finite-context model stream indefinitely at inference time. The resulting StreamingLLM framework lets Llama-2, MPT, Falcon and Pythia models do stable language modelling up to 4 million tokens and beyond with no fine-tuning, up to 22.2 times faster than the sliding-window recomputation baseline, and a dedicated sink token added during pre-training helps further. authors: Zechun Liu, Changsheng Zhao, Forrest Iandola, Chen Lai, Yuandong Tian, Igor Fedorov, Yunyang Xiong, Ernie Chang, Yangyang Shi, Raghuraman Krishnamoorthi, Liangzhen Lai, Vikas Chandra

title: LLM.int8(): 8-bit Matrix Multiplication for Transformers at Scale
authors: Tim Dettmers, Mike Lewis, Younes Belkada, Luke Zettlemoyer
institution: University of Washington; Meta AI; Hugging Face
verification: abstract read 2026-11-03; paper body left unread.
relevance: The first method to run 175-billion-parameter models in 8-bit with no accuracy loss. Inference memory is the binding constraint for large transformers, and naive 8-bit quantisation breaks at scale because of emergent large-magnitude outlier features that dominate attention and predictions. LLM.int8() combines vector-wise quantisation, with separate normalisation constants per inner product, with a mixed-precision decomposition that isolates the outlier feature dimensions (about 0.1 percent of values) into a 16-bit multiplication while more than 99.9 percent of values multiply in 8-bit. The result halves inference memory while retaining full-precision performance, so a 175B checkpoint can be loaded, converted to Int8 and used immediately, putting OPT-175B and BLOOM on a single server with consumer GPUs. The abstract is the record basis; the paper body was not read.

title: Algorithm appreciation: People prefer algorithmic to human judgment

title: Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2025
authors: International Energy Agency
verification: Executive summary verified at origin; full report left unread
relevance: IEA outlook on minerals for clean energy and digital technologies. China restricted gallium, germanium and antimony exports to the US in December 2024, with further 2025 restrictions, and the DRC suspended cobalt exports for four months in February 2025. A sustained battery-metal supply shock could raise battery pack prices 40-50%. China is the dominant refiner for 19 of 20 broader strategic minerals at about 70% average share, and capital costs in diversified regions run about 50% higher. LFP supply chains are more concentrated than nickel-based ones: China produces 75% of purified phosphoric acid and 95% of high-purity manganese sulphate.

Generation is rising five times faster than documented recycling: only 22.3% (14 Mt) was documented as properly collected and recycled in 2022, leaving US$62 billion of recoverable resources unaccounted for. Metals embedded in 2022 e-waste were worth US$91 billion, including copper US$19 billion, gold US$15 billion and iron US$16 billion, across 31 Mt of metals, 17 Mt of plastics and 14 Mt of other materials. Formal management reclaimed US$28 billion of secondary raw materials, avoiding about 900 Mt of primary ore extraction and 93 Mt CO2-eq, yet just 1% of rare earth demand is met by e-waste recycling. The documented rate is forecast to fall to 20% by 2030. Europe's formal rate was 42.8% and Africa's under 1%; Asia generates about half (30 Mt). Some 5.1 Mt was shipped across borders in 2022, about 65% from high-income to middle- and low-income countries undocumented. In 2023, 81 countries had e-waste legislation and 67 had extended producer responsibility.

title: Environmental impacts of rare earth elements mining and strategies for sustainable management: A comprehensive review

relevance: UNEP report on sand, the most used solid material at 50 billion tonnes per year and the second most used resource worldwide after water, linked directly or indirectly to all 17 Sustainable Development Goals. title: From FLOPs to Footprints: The Resource Cost of Artificial Intelligence
authors: Sophia Falk, Nicholas Kluge Correa, Sasha Luccioni, Lisa Biber-Freudenberger, Aimee van Wynsberghe

relevance: Preprint quantifying the material footprint of AI training by linking computational workloads to physical hardware. Combined software and hardware optimisation can substantially reduce material demands: increasing utilisation from 20% to 60% lowers GPU requirements by about 67%, extending lifespan from one to three years yields comparable savings, and implementing both together reduces GPU needs by up to 93%. Incremental performance gains, such as between GPT-3.5 and GPT-4, come at disproportionately high material costs. Only the abstract, introduction and methods were read, so later scenario results are not recorded.

title: The environmental impacts of deep-sea mining
authors: Adrian G. Glover, Maria Belen Arias, Guadalupe Bribiesca-Contreras, Jonathan T. Copley, Thomas G. Dahlgren, Jeffrey C. Drazen, Regan Drennan, Jeroen Ingels, Daniel O. B. Jones, Bryan J. O'Malley, Muriel Rabone, Eva C. D. Stewart
verification: Abstract verified at origin; full review left unread
relevance: Peer-reviewed review in Current Biology of decades of environmental research on deep-sea mining. The deep sea holds potential mineral resources investigated for commercial exploitation, starting in the late 1970s with polymetallic nodules in the Clarion-Clipperton Zone, and more recently seafloor massive sulphides at hydrothermal vents and cobalt-rich crusts on seamounts. Data from the Clarion-Clipperton Zone show the seafloor is biodiverse, albeit at low biomass. For nodule mining, geophysical and biological impacts are persistent over at least multiple decades, although some dominant animal groups show successional recolonisation. For sulphide deposits and seamounts, exploration has been quite limited, empirical data on recovery timescales are lacking, and these systems are likely to respond differently. Deep-sea mining in any habitat could generate plumes from ore dewatering that may affect pelagic ecosystems depending on the technology used. The review distinguishes ecological resilience and recovery from the risk of biodiversity loss through species extinction, finds clear evidence that biodiversity loss from deep-sea mining is likely at vents and, to some degree, seamounts, and argues that if such sites were classified as areas of high biodiversity importance under the Convention on Biological Diversity, deep-sea mining there would not be scientifically compatible with existing policy.

title: The Simple Macroeconomics of AI
authors: Daron Acemoglu
verification: Abstract verified at origin; full paper left unread
relevance: Task-based macroeconomic ceiling on AI's aggregate effect: so long as AI's microeconomic effects are driven by cost savings and productivity improvements at the task level, GDP and aggregate productivity gains can be estimated by what fraction of tasks are impacted and average task-level cost savings, by a version of Hulten's theorem. Using existing estimates on exposure and task-level productivity improvements, the effects appear nontrivial but modest, no more than a 0.66% increase in total factor productivity over 10 years. Adjusting for the fact that early evidence comes from easy-to-learn tasks while future effects come from hard-to-learn tasks with many context-dependent factors and no objective outcome measures, predicted TFP gains are even more modest, less than 0.53%. On distribution, even productivity gains for low-skill workers in certain tasks may increase rather than reduce inequality, there is no evidence AI will reduce labour income inequality, and AI is predicted to widen the gap between capital and labour income. Some new tasks created by AI may have negative social value, such as designing algorithms for online manipulation. NBER Working Paper 32487, May 2024.

title: The Economic Potential of Generative AI: The Next Productivity Frontier

title: New Frontiers: The Origins and Content of New Work, 1940-2018
authors: David Autor, Caroline Chin, Anna Salomons, Bryan Seegmiller
verification: Abstract verified at origin; remainder left unread
relevance: Eight decades of US Census job titles linked to Census microdata and patent-based measures of exposure to labour-augmenting and labour-automating innovations. New work emerges in response to technological innovations that complement occupational outputs and to demand shocks that raise occupational demand; innovations that automate tasks or reduce occupational demand slow new work emergence. Augmentation innovations strongly predict where new work emerges, while automation innovations do not, even though the two innovation flows are positively correlated. The demand-eroding effects of automation innovations have intensified in the last four decades while the demand-increasing effects of augmentation innovations have not. Quarterly Journal of Economics, 2024, vol. 139(3), pages 1399-1465; author-hosted paper read for the abstract and introduction.

title: Article 73: Reporting of serious incidents
authors: European Union

title: Overview and methodology of the AI Incidents and Hazards Monitor
authors: OECD.AI
verification: Methodology page verified at origin
relevance: How the OECD turns news coverage into an evidence base on AI harm after deployment. The AI Incidents and Hazards Monitor (AIM), developed by the OECD.AI expert group on AI incidents with support from the Patrick J. McGovern Foundation, tracks actual AI incidents and hazards in real time as an evidence base for policy, drawing on Event Registry, which processes over 150,000 news articles daily and clusters them into events tagged with AI concepts. The OECD states these publicly reported incidents are likely only a subset of all incidents worldwide. Definitions come from the May 2024 paper Defining AI incidents and related terms: an AI incident is an event where development, use or malfunction of AI systems directly or indirectly leads to injury or harm to health, disruption of the management and operation of critical infrastructure, violations of human rights or breaches of law protecting fundamental, labour and intellectual property rights, or harm to property, communities or the environment; an AI hazard is an event that could plausibly lead to an AI incident. Since November 2024 the pipeline retrieves events from Event Registry, filters them with language models (GPT-4o mini, then GPT-4o), classifies individual articles the same way with the event taking the most common article classification, generates metadata (title, summary, harm type, severity, affected stakeholders, country) with o3-mini from the top three articles, and clusters similar events by cosine similarity plus language-model assessment, running daily on events from one to four days ago. The page states both that on average about 1,000 AI events are analysed daily resulting in around 10 incidents or hazards, and that AIM detects on average 30 incidents and hazards per day; both figures are preserved as stated and not reconciled.

title: From deepfake scams to biased AI: How incident reporting can help us keep ahead of AI's harms

title: Regulation (EU) 2017/745 on medical devices: post-market surveillance and vigilance (Articles 83 to 88)

relevance: The EU medical-device model of post-market surveillance, the regime AI-enabled devices already live under. Article 83 requires manufacturers, for each device, to plan, establish, document, implement, maintain and update a post-market surveillance system proportionate to the risk class and appropriate for the device type, as an integral part of the quality management system, suited to actively and systematically gathering, recording and analysing relevant data on quality, performance and safety throughout the device lifetime, drawing conclusions and determining, implementing and monitoring preventive and corrective actions. Article 84 bases the system on a post-market surveillance plan, part of the technical documentation except for custom-made devices. title: Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2025/301: content and time limits for reporting major ICT-related incidents under DORA
authors: European Commission

title: Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Device Software Functions: Lifecycle Management and Marketing Submission Recommendations
authors: US Food and Drug Administration
verification: Guidance page and draft guidance text verified at origin
relevance: The FDA's total product lifecycle approach to AI-enabled devices after deployment, complementing the final PCCP guidance. This draft guidance, not for implementation and containing non-binding recommendations, issued 7 January 2025 under docket FDA-2024-D-4488 by CDRH, CBER and CDER, gives marketing submission recommendations for devices that include AI-enabled device software functions, reflecting a comprehensive approach to risk management throughout the device total product lifecycle. Section XI, Device Performance Monitoring, states the postmarket problem plainly: the performance of AI-enabled devices deployed in a real-world environment may change or degrade over time, presenting a risk to patients, and because models depend heavily on training-data characteristics, performance can be particularly sensitive to changes in data inputs, patient populations, disease patterns, or data drift, with users less likely to notice changes in highly automated processes or prognostic outputs. In general, as part of the quality system, manufacturers should have a postmarket performance monitoring plan to help identify and respond to changes in performance in a postmarket setting, and including such a plan in the marketing submission may help reduce uncertainty and support FDA's evaluation of risk controls. Manufacturers should proactively monitor, identify, and address device performance changes as well as changes to device inputs and context, and must develop and implement plans for comprehensive risk analysis programs consistent with the Quality System Regulation (21 CFR Part 820), while continuing to report deaths, serious injuries, and malfunctions under 21 CFR Parts 803 and 806. Sponsors that elect proactive performance monitoring as a means of risk control should include information about their plans in the premarket submission and are encouraged to obtain FDA feedback through the Q-Submission Program; for a 510(k) FDA generally does not require such plans absent certain circumstances, for a De Novo request such a plan may be necessary to control risks and FDA may establish a special control, and for a PMA such a plan may be a condition of approval, while sponsors may opt to include plan information in any submission. A robust plan identifies and responds in a timely fashion to performance changes, with data collection and analysis methods covering changes in model performance and their causes (patient demographics or disease prevalence, shifts in input data, input data corruption and integrity problems such as missing values, duplicate records and data type mismatches, and changes in user behaviour or demographics), robust software lifecycle processes including monitoring in the deployment environment, a plan for deploying updates, mitigations, and corrective actions in a timely manner (some actions may not require a marketing submission), and procedures for communicating monitoring results and mitigations to device users; the plan should sit in the Risk Management File in the Software Documentation section and does not replace statutory or regulatory requirements including Parts 803 and 806 reporting. title: Article 14: Human oversight
authors: European Union
verification: Article page verified at origin
relevance: The EU AI Act's human-oversight duty for high-risk systems. High-risk AI systems must be designed and developed, including with appropriate human-machine interface tools, so they can be effectively overseen by natural persons during their use, with the aim of preventing or minimising risks to health, safety or fundamental rights arising from intended use or reasonably foreseeable misuse. Oversight measures must be commensurate with the risks, level of autonomy and context of use, and are ensured through measures built into the system by the provider before placing on the market or putting into service, and/or measures identified by the provider for the deployer to implement. Persons assigned to oversight must be enabled, as appropriate and proportionate, to properly understand the system's capacities and limitations and duly monitor its operation, including detecting and addressing anomalies, dysfunctions and unexpected performance; to remain aware of the tendency to automatically rely or over-rely on the system's output (automation bias), in particular for systems providing information or recommendations for human decisions; to correctly interpret the system's output, taking into account available interpretation tools and methods; to decide in any particular situation not to use the system or to disregard, override or reverse its output; and to intervene in its operation or interrupt it through a stop button or similar procedure bringing it to a halt in a safe state. For remote biometric identification systems under Annex III point 1(a), no action or decision may be taken on the basis of the identification unless it has been separately verified and confirmed by at least two natural persons with the necessary competence, training and authority; that two-person requirement does not apply for law enforcement, migration, border control or asylum purposes where Union or national law considers it disproportionate.

title: Article 26: Obligations of deployers of high-risk AI systems

title: Article 27: Fundamental rights impact assessment for high-risk AI systems

title: OQ v Land Hessen (SCHUFA), Case C-634/21
authors: Court of Justice of the European Union
institution: Court of Justice of the European Union (EUR-Lex)
verification: Judgment verified at origin
relevance: The judgment that turned a credit score into an automated decision. The Court of Justice, First Chamber, 7 December 2023, quotes GDPR Article 22 in full: the data subject has the right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing, including profiling, which produces legal effects concerning them or similarly significantly affects them; exceptions apply where the decision is necessary for entering into or performing a contract, is authorised by Union or Member State law laying down suitable measures to safeguard rights, freedoms and legitimate interests, or is based on explicit consent; in the contract and consent cases the controller must implement suitable measures, at least the right to obtain human intervention on the part of the controller, to express a point of view and to contest the decision; and decisions must not be based on special categories of personal data unless Article 9(2)(a) or (g) applies with suitable safeguards. title: European Commission proposal to sign the Council of Europe AI Convention (COM(2024) 264)

title: A Right to a Human Decision
authors: Aziz Z. Huq
institution: University of Chicago Law School (Chicago Unbound)
verification: Abstract verified at origin
relevance: The sceptical case against a general right to a human decision. Huq starts from anxiety about a shift of power from human to machine decision-makers, as corporate and state actors increasingly lean on machine learning tools to allocate goods and assign coercion, from prison sentences to loan approvals to college applications. An emerging legal response is a right to a human decision, which European law has embraced in the GDPR and American law, especially in the criminal justice domain, is moving toward, yet no jurisdiction has defined with precision what that right entails or furnished a clear justification for it. Huq defines the conditions of technological plausibility for such a right as applied against state action, specifying the margins along which machine decisions are distinct from human ones, then tests three normative justifications: individual interests in participation and reason-giving; worries about insufficiently reasoned or individuated state action; and arguments based on negative externalities. His conclusion is that there is no general justification for adopting a right to a human decision by the state: concerns about insufficiently reasoned or accurate decisions are best addressed in other ways, and concerns about asymmetries of social power created by algorithmic tools are not parried by such a right. Available evidence instead tentatively points toward a countervailing right to a well-calibrated machine decision as ultimately more normatively well-grounded. Public Law and Legal Theory Working Paper No. 713; abstract read, full paper left unread.

title: Technological Due Process
authors: Danielle Keats Citron
institution: University of Virginia School of Law
verification: Abstract verified at origin
relevance: The founding argument that automated decision systems break both halves of administrative due process. Distinct procedures for adjudications and rulemaking lie at the heart of twentieth-century administrative law, with due process requiring notice and an opportunity to be heard. This century's automated decision-making systems collapse individual adjudications into rulemaking while adhering to the procedural safeguards of neither. They jeopardise due process norms: their lack of meaningful notice, and a hearing officer's tendency to presume a computer system's infallibility, devalue hearings. Standard Mathews v. Eldridge cost-benefit analysis is ill-equipped to compare the high fixed cost of deciphering a computer system's logic with the accumulating marginal benefit of correcting myriad inaccurate decisions. Automation also defeats participatory rulemaking, because code, not rules, determines adjudication outcomes, and programmers inevitably alter established rules when embedding them into code in ways the public, elected officials and courts cannot review. Citron argues a new concept of technological due process is essential, showing how a carefully structured inquisitorial model of quality control can partially replace aspects of adversarial justice that automation renders ineffectual, and providing a framework of mechanisms capable of enhancing the transparency, accountability, and accuracy of rules embedded in automated decision-making systems. Washington University Law Review, vol. 85, pages 1249-1314 (2008); abstract read, full article left unread.

title: Humans in the Loop

title: Algorithmic Accountability and Public Reason

title: Automation bias: a systematic review of frequency, effect mediators, and mitigators
authors: Kate Goddard, Abdul Roudsari, Jeremy C. Wyatt
institution: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association
verification: Abstract verified at origin
relevance: The evidence base for why human oversight fails: automation bias. Automation bias, the tendency to over-rely on automation, has been studied across academic fields; clinical decision support systems aim to benefit clinical decision-making, and although most research shows overall improved performance with use, there is often a failure to recognise the new errors such systems can introduce. This systematic review, with a healthcare focus, assesses the frequency and severity of automation bias, its effect mediators, and interventions potentially mitigating it, discussed alongside automation-induced complacency, or insufficient monitoring of automation output. Of 13,821 retrieved papers, 74 met the inclusion criteria. User factors such as cognitive style, decision support system, and task-specific experience mediated automation bias, as did attitudinal factors such as trust and confidence; environmental mediators included workload, task complexity, and time constraint, which pressurised cognitive resources. Mitigators included implementation factors such as training and emphasising user accountability, and design factors such as the position of advice on the screen, updated confidence levels attached to output, and the provision of information versus recommendation. Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association, 2012;19(1):121-127, DOI 10.1136/amiajnl-2011-000089; abstract read at PubMed, full review left unread.

title: Automation bias and verification complexity: a systematic review
authors: David Lyell, Enrico Coiera
institution: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association
verification: Abstract verified at origin
relevance: When oversight fails most: tasks that are hard to verify. Automation bias happens when users become overreliant on decision support, reducing vigilance in information seeking and processing. Most research originates from the human factors literature, where the prevailing view is that automation bias occurs only in multitasking environments. This review compares the human factors and healthcare literature, focusing on the apparent association of automation bias with multitasking and task complexity, drawing on EMBASE, Medline, Compendex, Inspec, IEEE Xplore, Scopus, Web of Science, PsycINFO, and Business Source Premier from 1983 to 2015. Of 890 papers identified, 40 met the inclusion criteria, 6 in healthcare. Contrary to the prevailing human factors view, automation bias was found in single tasks, typically involving diagnosis rather than monitoring, and with high verification complexity. Its limitations note the literature is fragmented, with large discrepancies in how automation bias is reported, and few studies reported the statistical significance of automation bias compared to a control condition. The conclusion is that automation bias appears associated with the degree of cognitive load experienced in decision tasks, and not uniquely associated with multitasking, so strategies to minimise it might focus on cognitive load reduction. Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association, 2017;24(2):423-431, DOI 10.1093/jamia/ocw105; abstract read at PubMed, full review left unread.

title: Street-Level Algorithms: A Theory at the Gaps Between Policy and Decisions
authors: Ali Alkhatib, Michael Bernstein
verification: Abstract verified at origin
relevance: Algorithms as street-level bureaucrats without reflexive discretion. Drawing on the theory of street-level bureaucracies, how human bureaucrats such as police and judges interpret policy to make on-the-ground decisions, the paper presents by analogy a theory of street-level algorithms: the algorithms that bridge the gaps between policy and decisions about people in a socio-technical system. The central challenge is that algorithms must bridge the gap between high-level policy and on-the-ground decisions, making inferences in novel situations where the policy or training data do not readily apply. Unlike street-level bureaucrats, who reflexively refine their decision criteria as they reason through a novel situation, street-level algorithms at best refine their criteria only after the decision is made, a loop-and-a-half delay: decision boundaries are effectively established beforehand, and the algorithm classifies test data without consideration of each case it encounters. The paper's framing therefore cuts directly against treating algorithmic deployment as equivalent to human discretion: the discretionary, reflexive adjustment that human bureaucrats exercise mid-decision has no algorithmic counterpart. CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems, May 2019, Glasgow, DOI 10.1145/3290605.3300760; abstract read, full paper left unread.

title: Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence

title: Ethics Guidelines for Trustworthy AI
authors: Independent High-Level Expert Group on Artificial Intelligence
verification: Guidelines page verified at origin; full Guidelines text left unread
relevance: The framework that gave human oversight its three canonical forms. Presented on 8 April 2019 by the High-Level Expert Group on AI set up by the European Commission, following a first draft in December 2018 that drew more than 500 comments through open consultation, the Ethics Guidelines for Trustworthy AI hold that trustworthy AI should be lawful, respecting all applicable laws and regulations; ethical, respecting ethical principles and values; and robust, both technically and in its social environment. Seven key requirements follow, beginning with human agency and oversight: AI systems should empower human beings, allowing them to make informed decisions and fostering their fundamental rights, while proper oversight mechanisms are ensured through human-in-the-loop, human-on-the-loop, and human-in-command approaches. The other requirements are technical robustness and safety, including a fallback plan in case something goes wrong; privacy and data governance; transparency, including that humans are aware they are interacting with an AI system and are informed of its capabilities and limitations; diversity, non-discrimination and fairness; societal and environmental well-being; and accountability, with auditability and accessible redress. The assessment list operationalising the requirements underwent a piloting process from June 2019, which closed on 1 December 2019, and the final Assessment List for Trustworthy AI (ALTAI) followed in July 2020. Only the Commission's Guidelines page was read; the full Guidelines text was left unread.

authors: European Union

A datasheet documents a dataset's motivation, composition, collection process, recommended uses, and so on, to improve communication between dataset creators and consumers and to push the community to prioritise transparency and accountability.

The paper argues adoption would help alleviate exclusion and bias in language technology, give better precision about claims of generalisability, and lead to language technology that meets users in their own preferred linguistic style without misrepresenting them.

Commercially open and closed datasets differ sharply in composition, with closed datasets monopolising lower-resource languages, more creative tasks, richer topic variety, and newer and more synthetic training data. Licences are frequently miscategorised on widely used dataset hosting sites, with licence omission above 70% and error rates above 50%. The audit is released with the Data Provenance Explorer for tracing and filtering data provenance.

authors: Samir Yitzhak Gadre et al.

The candidate pool is 12.8 billion image-text pairs from Common Crawl; participants design filtering techniques or curate new sources and evaluate by running standardised CLIP training and testing on 38 downstream test sets, across compute scales spanning four orders of magnitude. The best baseline, DataComp-1B, trains a CLIP ViT-L/14 from scratch to 79.2% zero-shot accuracy on ImageNet, outperforming OpenAI's CLIP ViT-L/14 by 3.7 percentage points with the same training procedure and compute.

relevance: The first image-text dataset of its scale made openly available: 5.85 billion CLIP-filtered image-text pairs, of which 2.32 billion contain English. Large language-vision models needed datasets of billions of pairs, and none of that size had been openly available to the broader research community. The paper shows successful replication and fine-tuning of CLIP, GLIDE and Stable Diffusion using the dataset, and also provides nearest-neighbour indices, a web interface for dataset exploration and subset generation, and detection scores for watermark, NSFW, and toxic content.

title: The RefinedWeb Dataset for Falcon LLM: Outperforming Curated Corpora with Web Data, and Web Data Only
authors: Guilherme Penedo, Quentin Malartic, Daniel Hesslow, Ruxandra Cojocaru, Alessandro Cappelli, Hamza Alobeidli, Baptiste Pannier, Ebtesam Almazrouei, Julien Launay

relevance: The case that curated corpora are not necessary for strong language models. Models are commonly trained on a mixture of filtered web data and curated high-quality corpora, and curation is believed necessary for broad zero-shot generalisation, but it is unclear how scalable curation is as models need trillions of tokens. Properly filtered and deduplicated web data alone can lead to powerful models, even significantly outperforming state-of-the-art models trained on The Pile. The authors obtain five trillion tokens from Common Crawl and publicly release a 600 billion token extract of RefinedWeb plus 1.3/7.5B parameter language models trained on it.

authors: Guilherme Penedo, Hynek Kydlíček, Loubna Ben allal, Anton Lozhkov, Margaret Mitchell, Colin Raffel, Leandro Von Werra, Thomas Wolf

relevance: A 15-trillion token dataset derived from 96 Common Crawl snapshots that produces better-performing language models than other open pretraining datasets, addressing the gap that state-of-the-art open models' pretraining datasets are not publicly available and little is known about how they were created. The paper carefully documents and ablates its design choices, including in-depth investigations of deduplication and filtering strategies. It also introduces FineWeb-Edu, a 1.3-trillion token collection of educational text filtered from FineWeb, whose models do dramatically better on knowledge- and reasoning-intensive benchmarks like MMLU and ARC. The datasets, data curation codebase, and ablation models are publicly released.

verification: Abstract verified at origin; full paper left unread
relevance: An open three-trillion token English corpus for language model pretraining research, built because information about pretraining corpora is seldom discussed: commercial models rarely detail their data, and even open models are often released without training data or reproduction recipes. Dolma mixes web content, scientific papers, code, public-domain books, social media, and encyclopedic materials, and is extensively documented, including its design principles, construction details, and contents. The paper presents analyses and experiments on intermediate states of Dolma about data curation practices and open-sources its data curation toolkit.

The Pile is constructed from 22 diverse high-quality subsets, both existing and newly constructed, many deriving from academic or professional sources. Untuned GPT-2 and GPT-3 struggle on many of its components, such as academic writing, while models trained on the Pile improve significantly over both Raw CC and CC-100 on all components and on downstream evaluations. An in-depth exploratory analysis documents potentially concerning aspects of the data, and the construction code is publicly available.

China is responding with domestic alternatives such as Huawei's Ascend series (lagging in performance and volume), stockpiling, smuggling, offshore datacentres, and CUDA alternatives, but these are not yet sufficient to overcome the controls' limits, though they may eventually form an alternative stack.

In 2023 Taiwan's semiconductor industry generated US$142.2 billion in production value, captured over 47 percent of global IC market share, and contributed near 30 percent of national exports and 15-20 percent of GDP. title: Nickel mining reduced forest cover in Indonesia but had mixed outcomes for well-being

In later production stages, environmental well-being continued to deteriorate substantially, especially in villages with already high poverty. title: What Investment Data Implies about the AI Transition
authors: Jessica A. Wachter, Jonathan D. Wachter
verification: Abstract read at origin (nber.org) 2026-11-04; full paper not read. Revised October 2026 per NBER page.
relevance: Uses firm investment data to size the AI transition. The authors report that five U.S. technology firms account for the majority of AI infrastructure investment, spending $404 billion (2022 dollars) in 2025, with 2026 spending forecast at nearly double that, and they argue these firms risk bankruptcy unless expected profits grow commensurately. A two-sector model with rare productivity booms, calibrated to investment through 2026, implies AI-sector productivity roughly tripled. Simulations with a two-year window and 50% annual chance of a repeat boom imply GDP gains by 2030 of 7% to 53%, with AI shares of GDP of 8% to 36%. The authors attribute the wide range to uncertainty about whether the boom repeats.

title: The AI Buildout and the Economy: Publicly Available Data to Assess AI's Impact
authors: Paul E. Soto, Mason Thieu, Jeffrey S. Allen
