AI-related components (software, data centers, power facilities, computer and peripheral equipment) contributed meaningfully to quarterly US GDP growth from 2025 through Q1 2026, though import drags offset much of the gross investment. Census BTOS data show adoption rising with firm size but shallow usage intensity, and early labor-market effects show up more as slower hiring of younger workers than layoffs. A companion XLSX with the underlying series is attached.

title: Artificial intelligence, firm growth, and product innovation
authors: Tania Babina, Anastassia Fedyk, Alex He, James Hodson

AI-investing firms show higher growth in sales, employment, and market valuations, driven mainly by product innovation rather than process automation. Results hold when instrumenting AI investment with firms' exposure to universities' supply of AI graduates. The authors report that growth benefits concentrate among larger firms and are linked to higher industry concentration, suggesting AI can fuel superstar firms.

title: Artificial Intelligence and the Labor Market
authors: Menaka Hampole, Dimitris Papanikolaou, Lawrence D.W. Schmidt, Bryan Seegmiller
verification: Abstract read at origin (nber.org) 2026-11-04; full paper not read. Revision date September 2025 per NBER page.
relevance: Constructs new task-level measures of workers' exposure to AI using natural language processing, covering 2010-2023 with variation across firms, occupations, and time. Tasks with higher AI exposure subsequently experience reduced labor demand. A model separates direct substitution from reallocative effects, and an instrument built from historical university hiring networks supports the causal predictions. Overall employment effects are modest: reduced demand in exposed occupations is offset by productivity-driven increases in labor demand at AI-adopting firms, per the authors.

title: The Labor Market Impact of Digital Technologies

In IT services, high-skill employment declined while high-skill vacancy postings rose, suggesting demand shifted toward newer skills. The authors conclude digital transformation brings both displacement and new opportunities. Korea-focused, useful non-US evidence.

title: The Exposure of Workers to Artificial Intelligence in Low- and Middle-Income Countries
authors: Gabriel Demombynes, Jörg Langbein, Michael Weber
verification: Abstract read at origin (openknowledge.worldbank.org) 2026-11-04; full paper not read.
relevance: Applies AI occupational-exposure measures to harmonized labor-force survey microdata from 25 countries covering a population of 3.5 billion people, using detailed 4-digit occupation codes. Within countries, exposure is higher for women, urban workers, and the more educated, but falls with country income: high exposure applies to just 12 percent of workers in low-income countries and 15 percent in lower-middle-income countries, and lack of electricity access limits effective exposure. The authors conclude labor-market impacts of AI in developing countries will likely be more limited than in high-income countries, and that higher exposure signals potential for change rather than inevitable job loss.

title: Buffer or Bottleneck? Employment Exposure to Generative AI and the Digital Divide in Latin America
authors: Paweł Gmyrek, Hernan Winkler, Santiago Garganta
verification: ILO publication page with detailed summary read at origin 2026-11-04; full paper not read.

The authors estimate 26-38% of jobs in the region are exposed to generative AI, with augmentation more likely than automation: 8-14% of jobs could see productivity gains while only 2-5% face potential full automation. Up to half of the jobs that could gain productivity (roughly 17 million, about 7 million held by women) are held back by digital-access gaps. Automation-exposed jobs tend to be urban, formal, higher-paid, and held by women, and in Brazil 8.5% of workers in poverty could benefit versus 14% of those not in poverty. The authors argue low digital inclusion will not buffer automation because most exposed workers already use digital tools.

title: Now Hiring: Firm-Level Adoption of Generative AI in China

By end-2025, 21 percent of listed firms but only 0.2 percent of non-listed firms had recruited GenAI-related roles, with adoption accelerating after the release of DeepSeek-R1. The authors discuss limitations of job-posting measures, including missing adoption via off-the-shelf tools.

The report notes middle-income countries accounted for half of ChatGPT's global traffic within six months of launch, that most workers in developing countries do manual rather than cognitive work so AI initially complements labour, and that a few firms in a handful of economies control frontier models, chips, and data centres, creating dependency risks. It casts governments as enablers, users, and regulators.

title: Use of Artificial Intelligence and Productivity: Evidence from firm and worker surveys

The author notes reliance on self-reported survey measures as an inherent limitation. Useful Japanese counterpart to US adoption studies.

title: Better Technology, Worse Motivation: Generative Artificial Intelligence's Mediocrity Trap
authors: Yvonne Jie Chen, Jie Gong, Jin Li, Zibo Zhao

The authors find AI improves output quality at every point but reduces the returns to continued effort, so many illustrators stop earlier and some submit lower-quality work than they would unaided. For developing economies hoping AI can compensate for scarce skills, they conclude productivity gains may require incentives and work design that sustain effort beyond the good-enough level.

title: Generative AI and Sales Productivity: Field Experiments in Online Retail

relevance: Large-scale randomized field experiments involving millions of users and products at a leading cross-border online retail platform, which deployed generative AI in seven business workflows (customer service, product matching, advertising, seller services) over 2023-2024. GenAI increased sales in most workflows, with effects ranging from no detectable impact to 16.3 percent depending on how much the AI added over existing practices; across the four positive applications the implied annual incremental value is roughly $5 per consumer. Gains come mainly from higher conversion rates rather than larger baskets, with no deterioration in return rates or customer ratings, and larger gains for less experienced consumers and smaller sellers.

title: The effects of generative AI on productivity, innovation and entrepreneurship

The authors flag research gaps on long-term business effects and on workers' understanding of AI's limitations. Useful as a curated map of the trial evidence base.

title: AI and Productivity in Europe

Europe's medium-term gains are around 1 percent cumulatively over five years, above Acemoglu's US estimates but varying widely across scenarios and countries, with substantially larger gains in higher-income countries. In a scenario where AI exposure falls 50 percent in regulated tasks, occupations and sectors, AI-safety and data-privacy rules could reduce Europe's productivity gains by over 30 percent, per the authors.

verification: Title page, abstract and introduction read from the published PDF (Stanford-hosted copy; the journal's DOI record lists the title with 'Copyright Law' and a published date of 5 June 2024) 2026-11-05. Full article not read.
relevance: The most-cited theoretical account of how generative AI strains copyright's foundations: Lemley argues that creativity will increasingly be lodged in asking the right questions rather than creating answers, so the idea-expression dichotomy and the substantial-similarity test for infringement both come under fundamental strain, and infringement doctrine may need to be rebuilt or applied in fundamentally different ways. He accepts that training foundation models is lawful while treating output-side liability as the harder problem. Reading it beside the Thomson Reuters v. Ross opinion sets early doctrine against the deeper structural critique.

title: Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model
authors: Rafael Rafailov, Archit Sharma, Eric Mitchell, Stefano Ermon, Christopher D. Manning, Chelsea Finn
institution: Stanford University, Columbia University, Carnegie Mellon University
verification: Abstract read at arXiv 2026-11-04; full paper not read. Verified v1 2023-05-29, latest v3 2024-07-29; title, authors and core claims checked against the arXiv page.
relevance: This is the training-method paper behind much of the post-2023 alignment of open and closed models. The authors show that instead of first fitting a separate reward model and then running reinforcement learning (RLHF/PPO), a language model can be aligned directly with a simple classification-style loss on human preference pairs. In their experiments DPO is stable, computationally lightweight, exceeds PPO-based RLHF on sentiment control and matches or improves it on summarization and single-turn dialogue. Its simplicity made preference tuning feasible for small labs and individual researchers.

title: QLoRA: Efficient Finetuning of Quantized LLMs
authors: Tim Dettmers, Artidoro Pagnoni, Ari Holtzman, Luke Zettlemoyer
verification: Abstract read at arXiv 2026-11-04; full paper not read. Verified abstract verbatim incl. the 99.3%-of-ChatGPT Guanaco claim and 'Extended NeurIPS submission' comment.
relevance: The paper that made fine-tuning of large models affordable on consumer hardware: gradients are backpropagated through a frozen, 4-bit quantised model into small low-rank adapters, so a 65B model can be fine-tuned on a single 48GB GPU. The authors introduce 4-bit NormalFloat, double quantization and paged optimizers, and report their Guanaco models reach 99.3% of ChatGPT's Vicuna-benchmark performance after 24 hours of single-GPU training. They also caution, via a 'lemon-picked' analysis, that current chatbot benchmarks are not trustworthy for judging chatbot quality.

title: Mixtral of Experts
authors: Albert Q. Jiang et al. (Mistral AI)
verification: Abstract read at arXiv 2026-11-04; full paper not read. Verified 26-author list, v1-only submission (2024-01-08) and Apache 2.0 release claim.
relevance: A widely cited open demonstration of sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) architecture, now standard at the frontier. Mixtral 8x7B routes each token to only 2 of 8 feedforward expert blocks per layer, so each token accesses 47B parameters while only 13B active parameters are used at inference. The authors report it matches or outperforms Llama 2 70B and GPT-3.5, with the largest gains in math, code and multilingual tasks, and released both base and instruction-tuned models under Apache 2.0. It teaches the core efficiency idea of decoupling total model capacity from per-token compute.

title: Scaling Data-Constrained Language Models
authors: Niklas Muennighoff, Alexander M. Rush, Boaz Barak, Teven Le Scao, Aleksandra Piktus, Nouamane Tazi, Sampo Pyysalo, Thomas Wolf, Colin Raffel
institution: Stanford University, Hugging Face, EleutherAI, Harvard University, University of Toronto
verification: Abstract read at arXiv 2026-11-04; full paper not read. Verified v1 2023-05-25 (latest v5 2025-06-28) and the datablations GitHub release of 400 training runs.
relevance: Asks what happens when the internet's high-quality text runs out — the central 'how much data is left' question in LLM scaling. From up to 900 billion tokens of experiments with 9B-parameter models, the authors find repeating data for up to 4 epochs causes negligible change in loss compared to fresh data, after which returns decay toward zero, and they propose a scaling law that prices in the reduced value of repeated tokens. Tested mitigations include adding code data and loosening common filters; models and datasets from 400 training runs are public. The paper underpins later debates about 'peak data'.

title: DataComp-LM: In search of the next generation of training sets for language models
authors: Jeffrey Li et al. (60 authors, DataComp-LM consortium)
institution: University of Chicago / TTI-Chicago with Stanford, MIT, Princeton, Hugging Face and others
verification: Abstract read at arXiv 2026-11-04; full paper not read. Verified the 240T-token corpus, 64% 5-shot MMLU at 2.6T tokens, and 6.6x compute-efficiency claims; distinct from the multimodal DataComp 2023 paper already in the library.
relevance: A community testbed that turns dataset curation into a measurable competition: it releases a 240T-token Common Crawl pool, standard pretraining recipes and 53 downstream evaluations so participants can compare filtering, deduplication and mixing strategies at 412M-7B scale. The authors find model-based filtering is the key lever, and their DCLM-Baseline set trains a 7B model to 64% 5-shot MMLU with 2.6T tokens, matching Llama 3 8B's average performance with 6.6x less compute. This is the clearest evidence that data quality, not just quantity, drives capability.

title: DeepSeek-V3 Technical Report
authors: DeepSeek-AI (Aixin Liu, Bei Feng, et al., ~200 authors)
verification: Abstract read at arXiv 2026-11-04; full paper not read. Verified 671B/37B parameters, 14.8T tokens, 2.788M H800 GPU-hours and the no-rollback stability claim.
relevance: The report that made the world recalculate frontier-training costs. DeepSeek-V3 is a 671B-parameter mixture-of-experts model with only 37B parameters activated per token, using Multi-head Latent Attention, an auxiliary-loss-free load-balancing strategy and a multi-token-prediction objective, pretrained on 14.8 trillion tokens. The authors report performance comparable to leading closed models at a total cost of only 2.788M H800 GPU-hours, with no irrecoverable loss spikes or rollbacks during training. It is a key primary source on efficiency-driven frontier training outside the US lab ecosystem.

title: Qwen2.5 Technical Report
authors: Qwen Team (An Yang, Baosong Yang, et al.)
verification: Abstract read at arXiv 2026-11-04; full paper not read. Verified the 7T-to-18T token pretraining scale-up, 1M+ SFT samples, and the Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct vs Llama-3-405B claim.
relevance: Documents one of the most downloaded open-weight model families, giving a concrete window into how a frontier lab scales pretraining and post-training. Qwen2.5 scales pretraining data from 7 to 18 trillion tokens and combines over 1 million supervised-finetuning samples with multistage reinforcement learning; the authors report the flagship Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct rivals Llama-3-405B-Instruct (roughly 5x larger) and that Turbo/Plus variants compete with GPT-4o-mini and GPT-4o on cost-effectiveness. Useful for seeing how data scale, SFT and RL are layered in practice.

title: GPQA: A Graduate-Level Google-Proof Q&A Benchmark
authors: David Rein, Betty Li Hou, Asa Cooper Stickland, Jackson Petty, Richard Yuanzhe Pang, Julien Dirani, Julian Michael, Samuel R. Bowman
institution: NYU Alignment Research Group with Stanford and UC Berkeley co-authors
verification: Abstract read at arXiv 2026-11-04; full paper not read. Verified v1-only submission and the 65%/34%/39% accuracy figures.
relevance: A deliberately 'Google-proof' benchmark of 448 expert-written multiple-choice questions in biology, physics and chemistry, built to stay useful even as models saturate older tests. Domain experts with PhDs score 65% (74% excluding mistakes the experts themselves identified), while skilled non-experts with unrestricted web access manage only 34% despite 30+ minutes per question, and the authors' strongest GPT-4 baseline reaches 39%. The asymmetry between expert and non-expert performance is precisely what makes GPQA the standard substrate for scalable-oversight experiments.

title: FrontierMath: A Benchmark for Evaluating Advanced Mathematical Reasoning in AI
authors: Elliot Glazer et al. (Epoch AI, 24 authors incl. external mathematicians)
verification: Abstract read at arXiv 2026-11-04; full paper not read. Verified v1 2024-11-07 (latest v7 2025-12-23) and the 'under 2%' solve-rate claim.
relevance: Hundreds of original, extremely hard research-level math problems written and verified by expert mathematicians, spanning number theory to algebraic geometry; a typical problem takes a relevant researcher hours, the hardest days. Unpublished problems plus automated verification limit data-contamination risk, and the authors report that state-of-the-art models at publication solved under 2% of problems — quantifying the then-huge gap between AI benchmarks and professional mathematical work. The benchmark later became a focal point for discussing how frontier-model progress is measured (and who funds and sees benchmark data).

title: Humanity's Last Exam
authors: Long Phan et al. (~1,178 authors across ~500 institutions)
institution: Center for AI Safety (CAIS) and Scale AI
verification: Abstract read at arXiv 2026-11-04; full paper not read. Verified the 2,500-question scope, v12 revision history (latest 2026-10-19) and the related Nature publication DOI noted on the page.
relevance: A crowdfunded, multi-modal 'closed-ended academic benchmark at the frontier of human knowledge' with 2,500 questions across dozens of subjects, each with an unambiguous, verifiable answer that is not quickly retrievable from the web. It responds to saturation — the authors note models now exceed 90% on benchmarks like MMLU — and reports that frontier LLMs score low and are poorly calibrated on it, exposing the gap between benchmark scores and expert-level reasoning. Published as a preprint with roughly 1,178 contributing authors; a version later appeared in Nature.

title: The Leaderboard Illusion
authors: Shivalika Singh et al. (Cohere Labs, with Princeton, Stanford, Waterloo, UW, Yale co-authors)
verification: Abstract read at arXiv 2026-11-04; full paper not read. Verified the 27-private-Llama-4-variants figure and the 19.2%/20.4%/29.7% data-share figures.
relevance: A systematic critique of Chatbot Arena, the most-watched LLM leaderboard. The authors document undisclosed private testing of multiple model variants with selective score disclosure (27 private LLM variants tested by Meta before the Llama-4 release), plus data asymmetries: Google and OpenAI received roughly 19.2% and 20.4% of all arena data while 83 open-weight models combined received about 29.7%. They show even limited arena-data access can yield relative performance gains of up to 112% on the arena distribution, and propose reforms — essential reading for understanding how evaluation incentives can distort what 'best model' means.

title: SWE-bench: Can Language Models Resolve Real-World GitHub Issues?
authors: Carlos E. Jimenez, John Yang, Alexander Wettig, Shunyu Yao, Kexin Pei, Ofir Press, Karthik Narasimhan
verification: Abstract read at arXiv 2026-11-04; full paper not read. Verified ICLR 2024 acceptance in the comments field and the 2,294-issue / 1.96% figures.
relevance: The benchmark that launched the coding-agent race: 2,294 real GitHub issues and pull requests from 12 popular Python repositories, where a model must produce patches that pass the project's own tests. Solving these requires coordinating changes across multiple functions, classes and files, and the authors found the best model at the time (Claude 2) resolved only 1.96% of issues. Its execution-based design — grading by whether the software actually works — has shaped nearly all later agentic evaluation, and the leaderboard at swebench.com tracks the field's progress.

title: AgentBench: Evaluating LLMs as Agents
authors: Xiao Liu et al. (22 authors; senior authors Minlie Huang, Yuxiao Dong, Jie Tang)
institution: Tsinghua University (THUDM / Knowledge Engineering Group) with Zhipu AI
verification: Abstract read at arXiv 2026-11-04; full paper not read. Verified ICLR 2024 acceptance, 8 environments, and the up-to-70B OSS-disparity finding; Tsinghua affiliation inferred from the THUDM GitHub release.
relevance: An early, influential multi-environment benchmark (8 distinct interactive settings) for judging LLMs as agents — testing multi-turn reasoning, decision-making and instruction-following rather than single-question accuracy. The Tsinghua-led authors found a large gap between top commercial models and open-source models of up to 70B parameters, traced failures mainly to weak long-horizon reasoning and instruction following, and showed better multi-round alignment data improves agent performance while code training has ambivalent effects. Released with open environments and an evaluation package.

title: OSWorld: Benchmarking Multimodal Agents for Open-Ended Tasks in Real Computer Environments
authors: Tianbao Xie et al. (17 authors)
institution: University of Hong Kong with Salesforce Research and University of Waterloo
verification: Abstract read at arXiv 2026-11-04; full paper not read. Verified the 369-task scope and the 72.36% human vs 12.24% best-model figures.
relevance: The first scalable benchmark that lets agents operate real computer environments (Ubuntu, Windows, macOS) rather than sandboxed mock-ups: 369 tasks across real web and desktop apps, OS file I/O and multi-application workflows, each graded by execution-based evaluation scripts. The authors report humans succeed on 72.36% of tasks while the best multimodal model of the time reached only 12.24%, failing mainly on GUI grounding and operational knowledge. It is the reference point for computer-use agents and for measuring how far they still are from human-level operation.

title: τ-bench: A Benchmark for Tool-Agent-User Interaction in Real-World Domains
authors: Shunyu Yao, Noah Shinn, Pedram Razavi, Karthik Narasimhan
verification: Abstract read at arXiv 2026-11-04; full paper not read. Verified v1-only submission and the '<50% task success, pass^8 <25% in retail' figures.
relevance: Targets the two things most agent benchmarks ignore: interacting with a (simulated) human user and following domain-specific policy rules. In τ-bench an agent with API tools and policy guidelines must serve an LLM-simulated customer in retail or airline domains, and success is graded by comparing the end-of-conversation database state to an annotated goal state. The authors introduce pass^k, a reliability metric for consistency across repeated trials, and report even top function-calling agents like gpt-4o succeed on fewer than 50% of tasks with pass^8 under 25% in retail — a quantification of agent unreliability that shaped later reliability debates.

title: The AI Scientist: Towards Fully Automated Open-Ended Scientific Discovery
authors: Chris Lu, Cong Lu, Robert Tjarko Lange, Jakob Foerster, Jeff Clune, David Ha
institution: Sakana AI (Japan) with University of Oxford and University of British Columbia
verification: Abstract read at arXiv 2026-11-04; full paper not read. Verified the <$15-per-paper and near-human-automated-reviewer claims and the SakanaAI/AI-Scientist open-source release.
relevance: The first end-to-end framework in which an LLM agent generates research ideas, writes and runs code, executes experiments, writes a full paper, and then reviews it with an automated reviewer, looping iteratively — demonstrated on diffusion models, language modeling and learning dynamics. The Japanese-led authors report each paper costs less than $15 to produce and that their automated reviewer reaches near-human performance in scoring papers. Widely cited both as a proof of concept for autonomous research agents and as a cautionary case study in agent reliability and the limits of automated review.

title: EAGLE: Speculative Sampling Requires Rethinking Feature Uncertainty
authors: Yuhui Li, Fangyun Wei, Chao Zhang, Hongyang Zhang
institution: Tsinghua University and University of Waterloo
verification: Abstract read at arXiv 2026-11-04; full paper not read. Verified the 2.7x-3.5x latency speedup / doubled throughput claim for LLaMA2-Chat 70B.
relevance: A leading speculative-sampling method that makes LLM generation meaningfully faster without changing outputs. Building on the observations that autoregression is easier at the feature level (second-to-top layer) than at the token level, EAGLE drafts feature sequences one step ahead to resolve uncertainty cheaply, then verifies with the original model. Across Vicuna, LLaMA2-Chat and Mixtral 8x7B models the authors report, for LLaMA2-Chat 70B, a 2.7x-3.5x latency speedup and doubled throughput while preserving the text distribution exactly. A concrete example of how much inference cost is pure engineering overhead.

title: FlashAttention-3: Fast and Accurate Attention with Asynchrony and Low-precision
authors: Jay Shah, Ganesh Bikshandi, Ying Zhang, Vijay Thakkar, Pradeep Ramani, Tri Dao
verification: Abstract read at arXiv 2026-11-04; full paper not read. Verified the 1.5-2.0x speedup, 740 TFLOPs/s FP16, ~1.2 PFLOPs/s FP8, and 2.6x-lower-FP8-error figures; distinct from the FlashAttention-2 paper already in the library.
relevance: Shows how tightly model capability depends on hardware-software co-design. FlashAttention-2 achieved only about 35% of the H100 GPU's theoretical peak on attention, so FA3 exploits Hopper-architecture features — warp-specialized asynchronous Tensor Cores and TMA, interleaved matmul/softmax, and FP8 support with block quantization and incoherent processing. The authors report 1.5-2.0x speedups, FP16 attention up to 740 TFLOPs/s (75% utilization), FP8 near 1.2 PFLOPs/s, and 2.6x lower numerical error than a baseline FP8 attention. The mechanisms that let long-context models be affordable at all.

title: The Era of 1-bit LLMs: All Large Language Models are in 1.58 Bits
authors: Shuming Ma, Hongyu Wang, Lingxiao Ma, Lei Wang, Wenhui Wang, Shaohan Huang, Li Dong, Ruiping Wang, Jilong Xue, Furu Wei
verification: Abstract read at arXiv 2026-11-04; full paper not read. Verified v1-only submission and the ternary {-1,0,1} weight formulation; abstract contains no specific benchmark numbers.
relevance: The Microsoft Research Asia paper behind the 1.58-bit idea: BitNet b1.58 replaces 16-bit weights with ternary {-1, 0, 1} weights, so each weight carries log2(3) ≈ 1.58 bits. The authors report it matches full-precision FP16/BF16 Transformer LLMs of the same size trained on the same token count in both perplexity and end-task performance, while being cheaper in latency, memory, throughput and energy, and argue it defines a new scaling law and recipe for training cost-effective LLMs. A central reference for low-precision and future-hardware debates, marked 'work in progress' by the authors.

title: How People Use ChatGPT
authors: Aaron Chatterji, Thomas Cunningham, David J. Deming, Zoe Hitzig, Christopher Ong, Carl Yan Shan, Kevin Wadman
institution: OpenAI and NBER (with Harvard University and Duke University co-authors)
verification: Abstract read at NBER 2026-11-04; full paper not read. Verified working paper number 34255, September 2025 issue date, and the 10%-of-adults / 53%-to-70% non-work / ~80% top-three-topics figures.
relevance: The most systematic look to date at how the general population actually uses a general-purpose AI product, based on a privacy-preserving automated pipeline over a representative sample of ChatGPT conversations from launch to July 2025, when the authors report adoption by around 10% of the world's adult population. Non-work messages grew fastest, rising from 53% to more than 70% of usage, work use concentrates among educated users in high-paid professional jobs, and the top three topics (Practical Guidance, Seeking Information, Writing) account for nearly 80% of conversations. Their conclusion that value flows mainly through decision support reframes debates about AI and productivity.

title: The Cybernetic Teammate: A Field Experiment on Generative AI Reshaping Teamwork and Expertise
authors: Fabrizio Dell'Acqua, Charles Ayoubi, Hila Lifshitz, Raffaella Sadun, Ethan Mollick, Lilach Mollick, et al. (with Karim Lakhani)
institution: Harvard Business School with Warwick Business School, Wharton, and Procter & Gamble
verification: Abstract read at NBER 2026-11-04; full paper not read. Verified working paper number 33641, April 2025 date, the 776-professional P&G setup, and the individual-AI-matches-team finding. A journal version later appeared in Organization Science.
relevance: A pre-registered field experiment with 776 Procter & Gamble professionals working on real product-innovation challenges, randomized to work with or without generative AI and alone or in two-person teams. Individuals with AI matched the performance of two-person teams without it; AI dissolved expertise silos, with R&D and Commercial participants producing equally balanced solutions; and participants reported more positive emotional responses when working with the AI. The authors conclude AI acts as a 'cybernetic teammate' and that organizations must rethink how expertise, teams and social connection are structured.

title: Which Economic Tasks are Performed with AI? Evidence from Millions of Claude Conversations
authors: Kunal Handa, Alex Tamkin, Miles McCain, Saffron Huang, Esin Durmus, et al. (15 authors)
verification: Abstract read at arXiv 2026-11-04; full paper not read. Verified the 4M-conversation scale, 36% of occupations at >=1/4 tasks, and 57% augmentation vs 43% automation figures; the paper underlies the Anthropic Economic Index launched February 2025.
relevance: The founding paper of the Anthropic Economic Index: a privacy-preserving analysis of over four million Claude.ai conversations mapped onto the US Department of Labor's O*NET task and occupation taxonomy. The authors find usage concentrates in software development and writing (together nearly half of all usage), about 36% of occupations use AI for at least a quarter of their associated tasks, and 57% of usage suggests augmentation of human capabilities versus 43% automation. They acknowledge the single-platform limitation, but the dataset and methodology give researchers an ongoing, granular window into AI adoption at work.

title: Scaling India's Data Centre Ecosystem: Stakeholder Perspectives on Infrastructure, Energy, and Resilience
authors: Vishal Tripathi, Debanjan Bagui, Prateek Aggarwal, Peter Hulshof, Arushi Chopra, Daksh Jain, Avantika Vashishtha
institution: CEEW (Council on Energy, Environment and Water) with SYSTEMIQ
verification: Publication page with executive summary and key-insight tables read at origin 2026-11-04; full PDF not read.
relevance: The most complete Indian energy-institute study of data-centre infrastructure, based on 24 stakeholder engagements. India's installed capacity nearly tripled from ~520 MW (2020) to ~1.5 GW (mid-2025) and could reach 4.5-6.5 GW by 2030, with committed investments of ~USD 95 billion (2019-25). Data centres use ~0.5% of national electricity and ~150 billion litres of water a year, both expected to more than double by 2030; Mumbai alone hosts ~25% of India's ~271 facilities. The authors find only 5 of 15 state data-centre policies embed sustainability provisions and recommend a national green data-centre framework and an integrated land-water-energy nexus approach. Stated basis is stakeholder consultation rather than metered facility data.

title: ASEAN Guide for Sustainable Data Centre Development
authors: ASEAN (no named authors in the pages read)
verification: Executive summary read from the full 77-page PDF at origin 2026-11-04 (pages 1-5); remainder of the guide not read.
relevance: An official 77-page regional policy guide for Southeast Asian policymakers and regulators navigating data-centre growth, developed through engagement with ASEAN Member States. It frames the problem as a 'Digital Infrastructure Trilemma' and reports that per-rack energy use is expected to jump from about 8 kW in 2021 to as high as 50 kW by 2027, straining grids and cooling, while ASEAN accounts for over half of the Asia-Pacific data-centre pipeline and its digital economy should exceed USD 1 trillion by 2030. It proposes four elements of sustainable development (energy/renewable integration via PUE, GHG reporting, plus water and others) and an ASEAN-level registry for PUE, WUE and renewable-share benchmarking aligned to the ASEAN Taxonomy for Sustainable Finance. Limitations: it is guidance, not binding regulation, and leans on 2025 Ember and industry pipeline figures.

title: AI and Energy: The Future of Data Centers in Saudi Arabia
authors: Khaled Alshehri, Marwa Mahmoud AlFattani, Laila Bashmal, Ghaliah Alshammari
institution: KAPSARC (King Abdullah Petroleum Studies and Research Center)
verification: Publication-page summary read at origin 2026-11-04; full PDF gated behind a name/email/organization registration form.
relevance: A Gulf energy think-tank briefing on AI-era data-centre growth, useful for the Saudi/Vision 2030 angle of the buildout story. The summary cites global data-centre capacity exceeding 111,900 MW in 2024 (US and China holding over 60%), expected to double to 224,000 MW by 2030, and global electricity use rising from 854 TWh (2024) to roughly 1,900 TWh by 2030. It notes AI workloads currently draw 5-15% of data-centre power, possibly reaching 35-50% by decade's end, and stresses that AI facilities differ from traditional IT through advanced chips, dense servers and liquid cooling. The visible summary does not give Saudi-specific figures; those are in the registered PDF.

title: The Geography and Geopolitics of Hyperscale
authors: Elizabeth Heyes
institution: Observer Research Foundation (ORF Middle East), Issue Brief No. 880
verification: Full issue brief read at origin 2026-11-04.
relevance: An Indian think-tank issue brief arguing hyperscale data centres (above 10 MW continuous load, some over 200 MW) have become strategic national assets, using a three-part framework of geographies of resources, infrastructure and data. It compiles the geographic constraints on siting - energy, water/cooling, fibre proximity, land, disaster risk - and cites a 2025 Virginia grid event as evidence that hyperscale demand can destabilise power networks. It links China's dominance of rare-earth mining (~60-70%) and processing (~90%) and TSMC's ~70% foundry share to which states can secure advanced compute, and reads the December 2025 US reversal of the H200 export ban through that lens. Recommendations include integrating hyperscale into national grid planning and classifying facilities as critical national infrastructure.

title: Não somos quintal de data centers (We are not data centers' backyard)
authors: IDEC (Instituto Brasileiro de Defesa do Consumidor)
institution: IDEC (Instituto Brasileiro de Defesa do Consumidor), Brazil
verification: Publication page read at origin 2026-11-04; the 118-page full PDF (idec.org.br/pdf/idec_estudo-nao-somos-quintal-de-data-centers.pdf) not read.
relevance: A Brazilian consumer-rights institute study of the socioenvironmental and climate impacts of data-centre expansion in Latin America, covering cases in Chile, Mexico, Uruguay and Brazil (press coverage cites the Quilicura, Chile case among them). The page argues big tech selects regions with cheap water and energy, weak environmental laws and little oversight, producing water shortages, higher electricity bills and projects approved without public consultation - a dynamic IDEC calls 'digital colonialism'. It also documents community resistance that blocked or forced revision of projects and proposes paths to digital sovereignty without sacrificing water and energy. Quantitative findings sit in the full PDF, not the page.

title: IEEJ Outlook 2026: AI and Future of Energy Demand
authors: Naoko Doi, Asamu Ogawa, Songhee Kim, Taichi Kusayagi, Soji Koikari, and other IEEJ authors
institution: The Institute of Energy Economics, Japan (IEEJ)
verification: Selected pages of the 27-page outlook presentation read at origin 2026-11-04 (title/outline and the data-centre demand outlook section); the 383-page full Outlook not read.
relevance: Japan's leading energy-economics institute devoted its flagship annual outlook to AI and energy demand. It estimates data centres at ~1.6% of global electricity consumption in 2023 with average PUE around 1.5, and projects global data-centre electricity demand more than doubling from 497 TWh (current) to 1,080 TWh by 2035 in the Reference Scenario. An Advanced Technologies Scenario (PUE improvement, ICT energy efficiency, better algorithms) could save 20%, reaching 865 TWh. It puts the data-centre share of final electricity demand at 2.9% to 7.2% (2023-2035) in developed economies versus 0.8% to 1.9% in emerging and developing economies.

title: Electricity Demand and Grid Impacts of AI Data Centers: Challenges and Prospects
authors: Xin Chen, Xiaoyang Wang, Ana Colacelli, Matt Lee, Le Xie
institution: arXiv preprint (eess.SY; Le Xie group, Texas A&M University and collaborators)
verification: Abstract read at origin 2026-11-04 (v6 revised 2026-08-04).
relevance: A power-systems review mapping how AI data-centre load stresses electricity grids. It characterises demand across the stages of model preparation, training, fine-tuning and inference, and organises grid challenges across three interrelated timescales: long-term planning and interconnection, short-term operations and markets, and real-time dynamics and stability. Solutions are surveyed from the perspectives of the grid, the data centres, and AI end-users. It is a synthesis/vision piece rather than new measurement, and the abstract page carries no headline numbers.

title: A Water Efficiency Dataset for African Data Centers
authors: Noah Shumba, Opelo Tshekiso, Pengfei Li, Giulia Fanti, Shaolei Ren
institution: Carnegie Mellon University Africa (arXiv; accepted NeurIPS 2024 workshop on Tackling Climate Change with Machine Learning)
verification: Abstract read at origin 2026-11-04 (v3 of 2026-06-12).
relevance: The first water-efficiency dataset for African data centres, filling a literature gap that focuses on rich countries. The authors combine national weather and electricity-generation data to estimate water usage effectiveness (WUE) for data centres in 41 African countries across five climate regions, and model inference water consumption for Llama-3-70B and GPT-4 in 11 countries - e.g., a 10-page report costs up to 0.66 litres via Llama-3-70B but up to ~59 litres via GPT-4, and for the same model 9 of 11 countries use less water than the global average mainly due to lower water intensity of electricity generation. The authors caution the estimates are 2024-modeled national reference values, not facility measurements, and note inference energy efficiency improved over 30x between May 2024 and May 2025.

title: Divergent Futures in a Damaged Territory: The Rise of Data Centers and Water Conflicts in Santiago de Chile
authors: Martin Tironi, Camila Albornoz
institution: Journal of Urban Technology, Vol. 32, Issue 4, pp. 51-68 (Taylor & Francis); Pontificia Universidad Catolica de Chile
verification: Metadata only (lead): Taylor & Francis returned HTTP 403 on 2026-11-04; bibliographic details (authors, journal, volume/issue, DOI 10.1080/10630732.2025.2546784) confirmed via search indexing; abstract not read.
relevance: A peer-reviewed STS/urban-studies article on the Google Cerrillos data-centre controversy in Santiago, the emblematic Latin American case of data centres colliding with urban water politics (Chile's environmental court partially revoked the permit in 2024 and Google paused the project over water worries; the original design reportedly drew 169 litres per second). It is the best academic anchor for local/community impacts and land/siting conflict in South America. Worth tracking down through a library since the full text is paywalled.

title: India's Semiconductor Ambitions and Global Competitiveness: Confronting the China Challenge
authors: Anulekha Nandi
institution: Observer Research Foundation, Occasional Paper No. 502 (Centre for Security, Strategy and Technology)
verification: Full occasional paper page read at origin 2026-11-04.
relevance: A detailed assessment of the USD 10 billion India Semiconductor Mission against China's chip rise. It documents India's dependence on China (trade deficit USD 99.2 billion in FY2024-25; China holds 98% of global gallium, 79% of raw silicon, 75% of ultra-high-purity silicon supply), China's 27-38% share of assembly/test/packaging and its USD 47.5 billion third Big Fund round. On India it details the Tata-PSMC fab at Dholera (28nm-110nm, first chips expected end-2026), the Chip-to-Startup programme (278 academic institutions and 72 start-ups with EDA tools as of August 2025), and argues for advanced-packaging 'leapfrogging' and a proposed India Semiconductor Research Centre.

title: Taiwan's Semiconductor Sustainability and Global Implications
authors: Chaouki Ghenai, Eugene Chausovsky
verification: Full article read at origin 2026-11-04.
relevance: A terrain analysis connecting Taiwan's chip dominance to its energy system: ~97% of Taiwan's energy supply is imported, and the 2023 grid was 42% coal, 40% LNG, 10% renewables, 6% nuclear. TSMC consumed nearly 25,000 GWh in 2023, and semiconductor electricity use is projected to be 236% higher than 2021 levels by 2030; wafer tools account for roughly 40% of a fab's power and facility systems (chillers, ultra-pure water, air handling) about 56.6%. It notes TSMC's 61.7% foundry share (Q1 2024) and its target of 25% green power by 2030, framing fab energy demand as a grid and climate problem for the island that fabricates most AI logic chips. Water figures are discussed qualitatively rather than quantified.

title: Chipping Point: Tracking Electricity Consumption and Emissions from AI Chip Manufacturing
authors: Greenpeace East Asia (credited authors Katrin W., Summer J., Rachel Y., and Alex de Vries)
verification: Executive summary and key findings read from the full 27-page PDF at origin 2026-11-04 (pp. 1-7); methodology appendix not read.
relevance: A bottom-up estimate of the electricity and emissions of AI chip manufacturing itself, a stage usually ignored next to data centres, and concentrated in East Asia (TSMC logic fabs in Taiwan; SK hynix/Samsung/Micron memory in South Korea and Japan). Key findings: global electricity for AI chipmaking grew from 218 GWh (2023) to 984 GWh (2024), up more than 350%, and could reach 37,238 GWh by 2030 - a 170-fold increase versus 2023, more than Ireland's total consumption. Emissions from chipmaking electricity rose more than fourfold in 2024 to 453,600 tCO2e, with Taiwan at 185,700 t and South Korea at 135,900 t, against grids that were 83.1% fossil in Taiwan and 58.5% in South Korea in 2023; it also flags approved LNG plants for SK hynix (1 GW, Yongin) and Samsung (3 GW). Estimates rest on public company disclosures and a bottom-up model, as the report's own disclaimer states.

title: Advancing Cloud and Data Infrastructure Markets: Strategic Directions for Low- and Middle-Income Countries - Chapter 5: Data Centers at the Core of Cloud and Data Infrastructure Markets
authors: Natalija Gelvanovska-Garcia, Vaiva Maciule, Carlo Maria Rossotto (book authors)
verification: Chapter abstract, main messages and opening pages read from the chapter PDF at origin 2026-11-04 (pp. 1-3 of 22); rest of chapter and other chapters not read.
relevance: The World Bank's flagship volume on cloud and data infrastructure, with this chapter as the clearest development-institution account of why data centres concentrate where they do. It identifies four investment factors - reliable affordable energy, resilient broadband, favourable geography/land, and a stable business environment - and warns that low- and middle-income countries lose out because of weak power and broadband. It quantifies the market: global data-centre spending was projected at US$222 billion in 2023, the number of hyperscale facilities reached 900 in 2023 (37% of worldwide capacity, forecast to exceed half by 2028), and the US had 5,375 data centres versus 448 in China in 2023. Analysis is market-level synthesis of industry sources (Synergy, Cloudscene) rather than primary measurement.

title: Power Hungry Processing: Watts Driving the Cost of AI Deployment?
authors: Alexandra Sasha Luccioni, Yacine Jernite, Emma Strubell
institution: ACM FAccT '24 (Hugging Face and Carnegie Mellon University)
verification: Abstract read at origin 2026-11-04 on the arXiv version (published at ACM FAccT '24, June 2024).
relevance: The most-cited academic measurement of AI inference energy, shifting attention from training to deployment. It offers the first systematic comparison of the ongoing inference cost of categories of ML systems, measuring the energy and carbon of 1,000 inferences on representative benchmark datasets, and finds multi-purpose generative architectures are orders of magnitude more expensive than task-specific systems even controlling for parameter count. The authors argue the pursuit of generality carries a steep environmental cost and release study data via an interactive demo. Based on benchmark measurement rather than production fleets, so it captures relative differences more reliably than absolute fleet totals.

title: Health-Informed Computing: Estimating and Addressing the Public Health Impact of Data Centers
authors: Yuelin Han, Zhifeng Wu, Pengfei Li, Adam Wierman, Shaolei Ren
institution: arXiv preprint (Caltech and UC Riverside; accepted at Communications of the ACM)
verification: Abstract read at origin 2026-11-04 (v1 of 2024-12-09, retitled in v4 of 2026-06-08; earlier version circulated as 'The Unpaid Toll').
relevance: The first systematic estimate of the public-health cost of data-centre air pollution (criteria pollutants from the electricity they draw), extending AI's environmental footprint beyond carbon and water. It projects the total annual US public-health burden of data centres to exceed USD 20 billion in 2028 driven by AI demand, and finds severe inequity: in the hardest-hit counties the per-household health burden is roughly seven times the national average while national aggregates stay modest. It proposes a 'health-informed computing' framework that allocates computing across space and time to cut health costs. Estimates are model-based projections for 2028 and depend on demand-growth and grid-composition assumptions.

authors: Greenpeace East Asia (project manager Tang Damin)

title: AI Energy Score (leaderboard and benchmark toolkit)
authors: Hugging Face AI Energy Score team
verification: Project README read at origin 2026-11-04; the leaderboard Space itself is JS-gated and was not read directly.
relevance: An Energy Star-style rating scheme for AI models launched at the February 2025 AI Action Summit in Paris, with a public leaderboard explorer (huggingface.co/spaces/AIEnergyScore/Leaderboard). Models are benchmarked on a standardised NVIDIA H100-80GB GPU across 10 tasks, grouped into classes (A small ~3B to C large), and awarded 1-5 star efficiency labels; outputs include GPU energy in watt-hours, tokens-per-joule, energy per prompt and CO2 emissions, with reasoning-effort modes comparable for text generation. title: Open Terrestrial Fiber Data Standard and Map ASA (P176146): Guide to Online Resources and Standard Development Process
authors: World Bank Digital Development Unit (with the International Telecommunication Union)
verification: Executive summary and background read from the full 24-page PDF at origin 2026-11-04 (pp. 1-4); annexes not read.
relevance: The founding guide for the Open Fiber Data Standard (OFDS), a global open standard for terrestrial fibre-optic infrastructure data developed by the World Bank with the ITU, piloted in Africa. It documents why connectivity data matters for AI-adjacent infrastructure: available fibre data is fragmented in format, scale and ownership, which hinders targeted, cost-efficient broadband investment decisions. The guide walks through the standard-development process (demand- and supply-side research, prior art, data modelling, schema, pilots, tooling) with resources on GitHub and the OFDS documentation site. It is process documentation rather than a dataset release, but the standard and map it describes are the open substrate for most terrestrial-fibre mapping since.

title: How Much of the United States Can Still Host New Hyperscale Data Centers? A Constraint-Based Feasibility Analysis
authors: Milan Janosov
verification: Abstract read at origin 2026-11-04.
relevance: A national-scale geospatial feasibility study of where US hyperscale data centres can still go, inferring feasibility from revealed siting patterns of existing facilities rather than demand forecasts or optimisation assumptions. It combines power-grid adjacency, environmental limits, land-use constraints and climatic constraints on a uniform hexagonal grid, and finds all approaches converge on a limited feasible land envelope far smaller than naive land-availability estimates. Headline result: total physically feasible US hyperscale capacity is in the tens of gigawatts rather than the hundreds. Results are grounded in present-day constraints and observed build-out, excluding future policy or technology change.

title: Africa's digital divide is closing, but participation in the digitalised economy remains highly uneven
authors: Shannon van Wyk-Khosa, Rosevitha Ndumbu, Matthias Krönke
verification: Findings summary read at Afrobarometer publication page 2026-11-05; full PDF not read (PDF fetch unsupported).
relevance: Policy Paper 95 from Africa's largest pan-African survey programme (Round 9, 39 countries, 2021-2023 fieldwork) documents the device, electricity and connectivity base that conditions who can participate in AI-era digital economies. Only 18% of respondents own a computer, 47% own a smartphone, 31% use the internet daily, and just 22% of households have grid electricity that works 'all of the time'; on average 42% of citizens have the devices, electricity and internet access needed for the digital economy. Readiness ranges from over 75% in Mauritius, Seychelles, Gabon and Morocco to roughly 10% in Malawi and Madagascar, with men, urban residents, youth and the better-off advantaged. Afrobarometer publishes its microdata openly, and Round 11 (launched 2026) is adding AI-related questions.

title: The scale of artificial intelligence literacy for all (SAIL4ALL): assessing knowledge of artificial intelligence in all adult populations
authors: María T. Soto-Sanfiel, Ariadna Angulo-Brunet, Christoph Lutz
institution: Hamad Bin Khalifa University (Qatar) with University of Barcelona and BI Norwegian Business School; Humanities and Social Sciences Communications
verification: Abstract and method summary read at Nature article page 2026-11-05; full text not read.
relevance: Peer-reviewed psychometric instrument for measuring factual AI literacy in the general adult population, built on Long and Magerko's framework in three phases (expert item rating; UK pilot n=501; two UK Prolific samples n=619 and n=393) to a final 56-item scale covering 'What is AI?', 'What can AI do?', 'How does AI work?' and 'How should AI be used?'. The authors report good fit (CFI/TLI >= 0.90 mostly), better internal consistency in Likert than true/false formats, and gender/education differences: men scored higher on recognising AI use and how AI works, and higher-educated participants scored higher on most dimensions. Stated limitations include UK-only samples, Prolific self-selection, and possible ceiling effects - so it still needs cross-cultural validation, but it is a ready-made open measure for comparative AI-literacy studies.

title: Citizens and Experts Unite: Final Report on Global Consultations for France's 2025 AI Action Summit
authors: The Future Society, CNNum, Make.org, Sciences Po Tech & Global Affairs, AI & Society Institute (ENS-PSL)

relevance: The largest documented global citizen consultation on AI governance to date: 10,000+ citizens and 200+ experts worldwide consulted between September and December 2024 to feed the Paris AI Action Summit, described by the organisers as the first such engagement in an AI summit's preparation. title: AI Diffusion in Low Resource Language Countries
authors: Amit Misra, Syed Waqas Zamir, Wassim Hamidouche, Inbal Becker-Reshef, Juan Lavista Ferres
institution: University of Maryland and Microsoft (arXiv preprint)
verification: Abstract read at arXiv 2026-11-05; full text not read.
relevance: Quantitative test of the claim that language is an independent barrier to AI inclusion: using a weighted regression that isolates the language effect from socioeconomic and demographic confounders, the authors find that countries dominated by low-resource languages have an AI-user share approximately 20% lower than their baseline characteristics would predict. The mechanism proposed is frontier LLM underperformance on low-resource languages due to training-data scarcity, which lowers practical utility and dampens adoption. Directly relevant to 'who is heard' - most of the world's ~7,000 languages are low-resource, so the paper links model coverage to measurable participation gaps.

title: The Levers of Political Persuasion with Conversational AI
authors: Kobi Hackenburg, Ben M. Tappin, Luke Hewitt, Ed Saunders, Sid Black, Hause Lin, Catherine Fist, Helen Margetts, David G. Rand, Christopher Summerfield
institution: University of Oxford (OII) and collaborators; published in Science
verification: Abstract read at arXiv preprint version (arXiv:2507.13919) 2026-11-05; the Science version is paywalled and was not read.
relevance: Large-scale peer-reviewed experiment on AI's persuasion capabilities: 19 LLMs deployed on 707 political issues with 76,977 participants, plus fact-checking of 466,769 AI-generated claims. The authors find AI-generated messages can be more persuasive than human-written ones, and that persuasive power comes mainly from post-training on persuasive data (up to +51%) and prompting strategies (up to +27%) rather than model scale or personalisation - and, strikingly, that more persuasive outputs were systematically less factually accurate. The authors conclude such capability is within reach of large and small actors alike, with direct implications for elections and information integrity.

title: A community-codesigned LLM-powered chatbot for primary care: a randomized controlled trial
authors: Sairan Li, Yanzeng Li, Shuya Zhou, ... Lei Zou, Shasha Han (Peking Union Medical College, Peking University, University of Glasgow, Tencent WeChat AI)
institution: Peking Union Medical College / CAMS and collaborators; Nature Health
verification: Full-text summary read at PubMed Central 2026-11-05.
relevance: Pragmatic double-blinded RCT (ChiCTR2500098101) of 'P&P Care', an LLM primary-care chatbot codesigned with community stakeholders via a dual-track role-play framework: 2,202 randomised and 2,113 analysed across urban and rural communities in 11 Chinese provinces (59.1% rural), comparing consultation plus e-learning modules vs consultation alone. The primary endpoint of objective health-need awareness was met (2.95 vs 2.34, P<0.001), all five consultation-quality metrics favoured the e-learning arm, and the chatbot outperformed recorded usual-care and telemedicine benchmarks on history-taking and diagnosis (4.13 vs 2.86 and 2.30). title: Large language model diagnostic assistance for physicians in a lower-middle-income country: a randomized controlled trial
authors: Imran Ahmed Qazi, Ali Ali, Ayesha U. Khawaja, M. Jahangeer Akhtar, A. Z. Sheikh, M. H. Alizai
verification: Abstract-level summary read at Nature article page 2026-11-05 (open access); full text not read.
relevance: Randomised trial (NCT06774612) testing whether GPT-4o access improves diagnostic reasoning for 60 licensed physicians in Pakistan - a rare LMIC setting for clinical AI evidence. After a 20-hour AI-literacy curriculum, physicians with LLM access scored 71.4% vs 42.6% for conventional resources alone (adjusted difference 27.5 percentage points, 95% CI 22.8-32.2, P<0.001) with no time penalty, and gains were largest for less-experienced physicians (+30.0 pp) and those with little prior LLM use (+46.4 pp). Notably, GPT-4o alone scored 82.9%, above physician+LLM, and the authors flag vignette-only design, a single model, and inability to separate curriculum effects from LLM-access effects as limitations.

title: How AI is used in FDA-authorized medical devices: a taxonomy across 1,016 authorizations
authors: Rohan Singh, Monika Bapna, Abdul Rahman Diab, Emily S. Ruiz, William Lotter
institution: Dana-Farber Cancer Institute / Brigham and Women's Hospital / Harvard Medical School; npj Digital Medicine
verification: Full-text summary read at Nature article page 2026-11-05 (open access).
relevance: Manual classification of all 1,016 FDA authorizations of AI/ML-enabled medical devices listed as of 20 December 2024 (grouped into 736 unique devices) - the most complete public map of what deployed clinical AI actually does. The authors report images dominate (621 devices, 84.4%, mostly radiology), 85.6% of devices do analysis vs 11.3% generation, quantification/feature-localisation is the largest AI function (65% of analysis devices) but is declining as a share (81% of new devices in 2016 to 51% in 2024) while triage and image enhancement grow, and no LLM-based devices appear on the list. title: AI tutoring outperforms in-class active learning: an RCT introducing a novel research-based design in an authentic educational setting
authors: Greg Kestin, Kelly Miller, Anna Klales, Timothy Milbourne, Gregorio Ponti
verification: Full-text summary read at Nature article page 2026-11-05 (open access).
relevance: Randomised crossover trial in Harvard's Physical Sciences 2 course (N=194 of 233 enrolled, Fall 2023) comparing a custom GPT-4-based tutor with pedagogical guardrails against the same course's in-class active-learning lessons. Students learned more than twice as much in less time with the AI tutor (median post-test 4.5 vs 3.5, p<10^-8; regression effect size 0.63 SD, quantile regression 0.73-1.3 SD) and reported higher engagement (4.1 vs 3.6) and motivation, with 83% rating AI explanations as good as or better than human instructors'. The authors explicitly caution against AI replacing class time: results cover initial learning at understanding/applying levels, depended on instructor-written solutions to limit hallucinations, and higher-order synthesis was not assessed.

title: From Chalkboards to Chatbots: Evaluating the Impact of Generative AI on Learning Outcomes in Nigeria
authors: Martin De Simone, Federico Tiberti, Maria Barron Rodriguez, Federico Manolio, Wuraola Mosuro, Eliot Jolomi Dikoru
institution: World Bank (Policy Research Working Paper No. 11125)
verification: Abstract read at World Bank Open Knowledge Repository 2026-11-05; full 51-page PDF not read.
relevance: One of the first RCTs of generative AI as a school tutor in a developing country: a six-week after-school programme using Microsoft Copilot (GPT-4) for English learning among first-year senior secondary students in Nigeria. title: Venture capital investments in artificial intelligence through 2025

Useful for mapping where AI startup funding flows by country and funding stage, with the caveat that the landing-page abstract does not quantify totals.

title: Government as Venture Capitalists in AI
authors: Martin Beraja, Wenwei Peng, David Y. Yang, Noam Yuchtman

The authors find government funds are distributed more widely across space than private funds and back firms with weaker pre-investment performance signals — yet those firms grow faster than private-VC-backed firms. Private VC funds tend to invest after government VCs, especially when a firm's hometown government fund makes direct investments in weaker-signal firms. Read through the lens of VC's role in overcoming information frictions under China's institutional constraints; a rare large-scale dataset on state-directed AI investment.

title: Financing the AI Buildout
authors: Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh
institution: NBER (Working Paper 35865); forthcoming Brookings Papers on Economic Activity, Fall 2026
verification: Abstract read at origin (nber.org) 2026-11-05; full paper not read. Issue date October 2026 per NBER page.
relevance: Sizes and maps the financing of AI infrastructure: the abstract estimates a 1 GW AI campus costs roughly $41 billion and that completing a 188 GW US buildout by 2032 would require nearly $9 trillion of total investment, equal to annual investment of about 3.2 percent of GDP over 2025-2032. As hyperscaler capital expenditures exceed internal cash flow, financing shifts toward leases, joint ventures, project debt, private credit, securitization and special-purpose vehicles, which broaden capacity but raise asset-level leverage and obscure contingent obligations. The author flags tenant concentration, technological obsolescence, execution delays and uncertain residual values as risks. A finance-oriented companion to capex-discussion sources.

Using company filings through August 2026, it documents cloud revenue as early return on investment (AWS +37% year-on-year with a $496 billion backlog; Azure +43%; Google Cloud +82% with $514 billion backlog; Oracle cloud revenue rising from $2.1 billion in Q1 2025 to $5.8 billion in Q4 2026) and a financing shift from free cash flow to debt and equity, including Alphabet's $85 billion equity raise in June 2026. Bottlenecks cited include power (data centers at 9-17 percent of US electricity demand by 2030, up from 3-4 percent) and a DRAM shortage. title: World Trade Report 2025: Making trade and AI work together to the benefit of all
authors: World Trade Organization

Chapters cover the trade-AI relationship, domestic policies that shape it, and international cooperation, with the WTO's role framed as administering rules, fostering dialogue and transparency, and building capacity. The global-policy counterpart to empirical AI-trade papers.

title: Through the looking glass: artificial intelligence, international trade, and economic growth in the long run
authors: Eddy Bekkers, Lee Humphreys, Hryhorii Kalachyhin, Karolina Wilczynska, Danchen Zhao
institution: World Trade Organization (Staff Working Paper ERSD-2025-09)

relevance: Quantitative multi-sector, multi-factor trade model in which AI reallocates tasks from labour to AI services, raising productivity and cutting trade costs, with four scenarios varying how fast less-prepared economies catch up. Returns shift toward capital and the skill premium declines, though all factors gain in real terms. The authors caution the estimates are scenario-dependent and note low- and middle-income economies capture more gains with better digital infrastructure and broad AI deployment.

title: Artificial Intelligence and International Trade in Services: Evidence from the United States
authors: Paulo Bastos, Gaurav Nayyar
institution: World Bank (Development Research Group, draft supported by the Umbrella Facility for Trade trust fund)

relevance: First-pass causal evidence that AI adoption reshapes trade in services rather than only domestic jobs: using bilateral US services trade data for 2011-2024 with OLS and an IV strategy (occupational AI exposure interacted with nationwide AI adoption), the authors find US services sectors with stronger AI adoption increased exports more, to both developed and developing economies. They find no robust evidence that AI adoption reduces services imports, suggesting AI is not systematically replacing services sourced from other countries. Grounded in the Artuc-Bastos-Rijkers (2023) two-stage-production Ricardian model; limitations include the US-only setting and adoption measured by exposure proxies. Directly relevant to offshoring and outsourcing fears for developing-country service exporters.

title: The Algorithmic Human Manager: AI, Apps, and Workers in the Indian Gig Economy

relevance: India-focused, mixed-methods study of AI-mediated management of blue-collar gig workers (ride-sharing, delivery, home services), based on in-depth interviews with 16 gig workers and 21 key stakeholders within a social-justice framework. Workers experience the app as 'the manager' but believe humans behind the curtain make the real decisions, and report opaque task allocation, stage determination, pay structures and penalties beyond their control; stakeholders describe practices such as 'algorithmic cruelty' via manipulated incentives and deactivations without due process. The report situates findings in India's policy landscape (Code on Social Security 2020 not yet notified; state-level measures in Rajasthan, Karnataka, Jharkhand, Bihar and Telangana). Small qualitative sample, but rare primary evidence from the worker side in a major gig economy.

title: Exposure to Artificial Intelligence and Occupational Mobility: A Cross-Country Analysis
authors: Mauro Cazzaniga, Carlo Pizzinelli, Emma Rockall, Marina M. Tavares
institution: Economia LACEA Journal, vol. 24, issue 1, pp. 314-339 (authors affiliated with the IMF)
verification: Abstract and key findings read at origin (economia.lse.ac.uk) 2026-11-05. DOI 10.31389/eco.451.
relevance: Open-access study of workers' occupational transitions in Brazil and the UK, classifying jobs by AI exposure and complementarity (high-exposure/high-complementarity, high-exposure/low-complementarity, low-exposure). Over 85 percent of college-educated workers in both countries are in high-exposure occupations; the UK has 35 percent of employment in high-exposure/high-complementarity jobs versus 19 percent in Brazil, and college education raises the probability of moving into such jobs by 11.4 percentage points in Brazil versus 2.26 in the UK. Simulations suggest destroying all high-exposure/low-complementarity jobs would cut lifetime earnings by 27.9 percent for college and 31.7 percent for non-college workers in Brazil. Brazil's much higher quarterly occupational switching (33 percent versus 12 percent) and 42 percent informality are the key institutional differences; mobility data are survey-based and pre-date large-scale generative AI.

title: Interactions of Artificial Intelligence with India's Labour Market: Devising an AI-for-Labour Model using the Productivity, Inclusivity, and Entrepreneurship Framework

The authors conclude AI diffusion in India will be uneven: displacement risk is limited for now in employment-intensive, low-productivity sectors, but exclusion from AI-enabled productivity gains is the bigger concern; manufacturing can upgrade through servicification; knowledge-intensive services face augmentation requiring high-level skilling. Argues for a diffusion-first AI strategy built on skills, infrastructure and institutions. Desk-based synthesis rather than causal estimation.

title: South Asia Development Update, October 2025: Jobs, AI, and Trade — Chapter 2: Artificial Intelligence, Real Impact: Labor Market Implications of AI Adoption in South Asia

relevance: Flagship regional report chapter quantifying AI exposure in South Asia using occupation-level measures and job-listings data. Only 7 percent of South Asia's jobs are highly exposed to AI without complementarity (at automation risk), well below the 15 percent exposure in other emerging markets, while the 15 percent of workers in jobs with strong AI complementarities could see substantial productivity gains. Jobs requiring AI skills command a wage premium of nearly 30 percent relative to other white-collar jobs, and generative AI has already reduced monthly job listings by around 20 percent for the most exposed and most substitutable white-collar occupations, with largest losses in business services and IT among upper-middle-skilled and entry-level workers. Exposure estimates rest on US-derived task measures applied to the region, a limitation the report acknowledges.

title: Adoption of artificial intelligence in Spanish firms: an initial analysis based on the Banco de España Business Activity Survey
authors: Alejandro Fernández Cerezo, Ignacio Hidalgo, Mario Izquierdo

relevance: Central-bank survey evidence on AI adoption in Spain using the Banco de España Business Activity Survey (EBAE). Adoption is highest in technology services and among large, productive and young firms; the main barriers are lack of skilled labour, high implementation costs and data availability; uses concentrate on optimizing internal processes and marketing rather than automation or innovation. Notably, 80 percent of firms believe AI will not affect employment, and firms already using AI expect a positive employment impact.

title: Artificial intelligence in UK businesses: 2023 to 2026

verification: Article read at origin (ons.gov.uk) 2026-11-05.
relevance: Official UK time series on business AI use, usable to benchmark adoption claims. AI use among UK businesses with 10 or more employees rose from roughly 12 percent in late 2023 to about 35 percent by June 2026, with 49 percent of firms with 250+ employees using AI versus 28 percent of firms with 0-9 employees. Large language models were the most used technology (18 percent), information and communication the leading industry (58 percent), and improving business operations the most common purpose (around 60 percent of users). Most adopting firms reported no headcount change (about 6 percent of medium-sized firms reported decreases), and 41 percent of businesses reported no adoption barriers.

title: Artificial intelligence adoption and productivity in Canadian firms

AI adopters show 16.8 percent higher labour productivity than non-adopters, but the premium falls to 10.2 percent controlling for pre-adoption productivity, and to a statistically insignificant 5.1 percent once complementary capabilities (R&D, cloud computing, data analytics, robotics, ICT training) are added; no significant link to short-term productivity growth. The authors conclude AI pays off only when embedded in broader digital-transformation strategies — a cautionary benchmark for headline adoption-productivity claims.

title: AI adoption in America: Who, what, and where

Adoption clustered with cloud computing and robotics, was higher among young firms with venture funding and high-growth signals, and was geographically concentrated in a few superstar cities — the base dataset for much subsequent US firm-level AI research.

SME AI adoption tripled from 4.2 percent in 2023 to 14.5 percent in 2024, driven mainly by off-the-shelf generative AI tools, while non-SME adoption rose from 44.0 percent to 62.5 percent; the digital economy reached S$128.1 billion, 18.6 percent of GDP. A companion IMDA pulse survey found 73.8 percent of surveyed workers use AI tools at work, 85 percent of AI users reported productivity, time-saving or quality improvements, and the share of tech job postings requiring AI skills rose from 11 percent in 2019 to 14 percent in 2024. Based on IMDA's annual enterprise survey methodology, so self-reported.

title: Economic Growth under Transformative AI
authors: Philip Trammell, Anton Korinek
institution: NBER (Working Paper 31815); published in the Annual Review of Economics, vol. 18 (2026)

relevance: The standard synthesis of growth models under transformative AI, reviewing what happens if machines can automate essentially all work. Robustly, full automation of production (machine self-replication) would dramatically raise growth rates and lower the labour share, breaking the Kaldor Facts; automating R&D (machine self-improvement) would accelerate the transformation but may not produce it alone. Wages — the product of exploding output and a plummeting labour share — may rise or fall depending on returns to scale, natural resources, and the direction of technical change. A framework paper rather than new empirics; useful as the map of AGI-growth modelling assumptions.

title: We Won't be Missed: Work and Growth in the AGI World
authors: Pascual Restrepo

relevance: A formal model of long-run growth and wages once artificial general intelligence can perform all economically valuable work with compute. The author distinguishes bottleneck work (essential for growth) from supplementary work, and shows the economy eventually automates all bottleneck work, output becomes linear in compute and labour, growth is driven by compute expansion, wages converge to the opportunity cost of the compute needed to replicate human work, and the labour share of income converges to zero. Even post-AGI, positive wages persist for skills that save compute and for supplementary tasks left to humans. Pure theory with stark distributional implications; no data.

title: Miracle or Myth? Assessing the macroeconomic productivity gains from Artificial Intelligence
authors: Francesco Filippucci, Peter Gal, Matthias Schief

relevance: A micro-to-macro reconciliation of why AI productivity forecasts diverge: the authors combine micro-level performance-gain estimates with evidence on AI exposure and likely adoption rates, aggregating through a multi-sector general equilibrium model with input-output linkages over a 10-year horizon. Their central estimate is annual aggregate total-factor productivity growth from AI of 0.25-0.6 percentage points, rising to 0.4-0.9 percentage points for labour productivity. The paper analyzes the channels shaping gains (adoption speed, complementarities, reallocation) and highlights policy levers. The benchmark 'sober middle' scenario between boom and scepticism in the Solow-paradox debate.

title: AI innovation and the labor share in European regions
authors: Antonio Minniti, Klaus Prettner, Francesco Venturini

relevance: Peer-reviewed evidence that AI innovation shifts income from labour to capital within European regions, using regional data from 2000 onwards. Each doubling of regional AI innovation reduces the labour share by 0.5 to 1.6 percent, which the authors translate into a reduction of 0.09 to 0.31 percentage points from an average labour share of 52 percent attributable to AI. The technology harms high- and medium-skill workers most, mainly through wage compression, while AI-induced employment growth slightly offsets wage declines for low-skill workers. Effects are robust to excluding other regional development drivers and AI-market concentration; identification is correlational with fixed effects rather than experimental.

title: The Rise of Industrial AI in America: Microfoundations of the Productivity J-curve(s)
authors: Kristina McElheran (University of Toronto), Mu-Jeung Yang (University of Oklahoma), Zachary Kroff, Erik Brynjolfsson (Stanford University)
institution: US Census Bureau, Center for Economic Studies (CES Working Paper 25-27)
verification: Title page, abstract and introduction read from the 56-page PDF 2026-11-05; full paper not read.
relevance: Census working paper providing the causal micro-foundations for the AI productivity J-curve — the modern Solow paradox. Using two waves of large-scale data collected with the Census Bureau for 2017 and 2021 on AI in American manufacturing, the authors find short-term performance losses (harming productivity and profitability, raising work-in-progress inventory, robot investment and labour shedding) that precede longer-term gains, concentrated among older businesses and mitigated by growth-oriented strategies and within-firm spillovers. Abandonment of structured production-management practices accounts for roughly one-third of the short-run losses among older establishments, identifying a specific intangible-capital channel. Pre-2017 adopters exhibit stronger growth conditional on survival; results are manufacturing-specific and cover the pre-generative-AI wave.

title: Resolução No. 23.732, de 27 de fevereiro de 2024 (amendments to Res.-TSE No. 23.610/2019 on electoral propaganda: AI, deepfakes and internet-platform duties)

It also creates platform duties: anti-disinformation terms of use, notification and reporting channels, ad repositories searchable via API (Art. 27-A), joint liability for failure to remove, and even election-focused data-protection impact assessments for large campaigns (Art. 33-D). A labelling-plus-liability model built by an election court rather than a legislature, distinct from both the EU and US approaches.

title: Altered Video of President Biden - Meta Oversight Board decision and recommendations on manipulated media policy

It recommended a method-agnostic policy covering audio and depictions of people doing things they did not do, harms defined around voting rights, and labelling instead of removal absent another violation, with urgency given the 2024 global election year. Violations are channelled to existing law such as the Electronic Information and Transactions Law rather than AI-specific penalties. A representative case of soft-law first steps in Southeast Asia: fast to issue, low in coercive force, and a marker against which Indonesia's later PDP-law enforcement and AI policy can be measured.

title: Opinion 28/2024 on certain data protection aspects related to the processing of personal data in the context of AI models
authors: European Data Protection Board (adopted at the request of the Irish Data Protection Commission)
verification: EDPB press release read at origin 2026-11-05: Opinion adopted in Brussels on 18 December 2024; the three questions (anonymity, legitimate interest, consequences of unlawful processing in development) and key conclusions summarised were read directly. Full 35-page opinion PDF not read.
relevance: The EDPB's most consequential statement on how the GDPR applies to AI models, requested by the Irish DPC to promote harmonisation across EU regulators. It holds that models trained on personal data cannot be presumed anonymous (case-by-case assessment of memorisation and extraction risk); that legitimate interest can generally serve as the legal basis for developing and deploying AI models only through a strict three-step necessity-and-balancing test with mitigating measures; and that processing personal data unlawfully during development can taint the lawfulness of downstream deployment unless the model is duly anonymised. The opinion has become the reference point for GDPR-AI compliance debates and supervisory practice. Limitations: it is guidance, not law, and leaves hard questions to national DPAs' case-by-case analysis.

relevance: Brazil's data protection authority used its new LGPD powers to suspend Meta's plan to train generative AI on the personal data of Brazilians (Facebook alone has about 102 million Brazilian users), finding that a 'legitimate interest' basis could not cover sensitive data, that users could not expect old posts to train AI that did not exist when posted, that opt-out obstacles were excessive, and that children's data lacked the required best-interest safeguards. The authority acted ex officio within days of the policy change, invoking grave and irreversible harm. Widely studied as the leading Global-South enforcement action on AI training data; secondary reports indicate the restriction was lifted in late August 2024 after Meta presented adjustments, which makes it equally a case study in the negotiation between regulators and platforms.
