relevance: In May 2025 Kenya's High Court declared Worldcoin's collection of Kenyans' iris and facial scans unlawful under the Data Protection Act 2019 and the Constitution: consent bought with roughly KES 7,000 in cryptocurrency was not free, specific or informed ('luring poor Kenyans with cryptocurrency bypasses the essence of informed consent'); no data protection impact assessment was done for high-risk biometric processing; data moved to servers abroad without required safeguards; and local processors were unregistered. The court ordered permanent, supervised erasure of the biometric data and a halt to collection, building on the ODPC's 2023 determination against Worldcoin entities. The most consequential biometric-surveillance ruling from Africa, now a reference point for data sovereignty and consent standards in the Global South.

title: Toolkit for Responsible AI Innovation in Law Enforcement
authors: INTERPOL Innovation Centre and the United Nations Interregional Crime and Justice Research Institute (UNICRI), funded by the European Union
verification: INTERPOL Innovation AI Toolkit page read at origin 2026-11-05: published June 2023, developed by INTERPOL with UNICRI with EU funding, comprising seven resources plus a user guide and to be implemented through training, cooperative projects and the INTERPOL Responsible AI Lab (I-RAIL); a revised toolkit was announced 6 March 2024 per the Innovation page.
relevance: The first global governance toolkit for police adoption of AI, produced by INTERPOL and UNICRI to help law-enforcement agencies institutionalise responsible AI across development, procurement and use. Its seven resources include AI principles for policing, a technical reference book, risk-assessment questionnaires, an organisational roadmap and a workbook, covering use cases from emergency call centres to identifying exploited children while stressing human-rights and policing-principle safeguards, with particular attention to generative AI risks. It matters because most AI-governance debates regulate private-sector AI, while state coercion uses of AI (predictive policing, biometrics, triage) are governed mainly through voluntary frameworks like this one. Limitation: non-binding, and uptake varies widely across INTERPOL's 196 member countries.

title: Smart Justice? Making Sense of the Rise of Algorithm-Based Pre-trial Risk Assessment in Criminal Justice Through 'Legal Models'
authors: Georg Wenzelburger, Karen Yeung, Kathrin Hartmann
institution: Digital Society (Springer), vol. 4, no. 2; Saarland University and University of Birmingham
verification: OpenAlex record for DOI 10.1007/s44206-025-00194-7 read 2026-11-05 (title, authors, affiliations, publication date 11 June 2025, open-access status and abstract); the Springer article page itself was unreachable through automated fetch (cookie redirect).
relevance: A legal-theoretical analysis of the wave of US 'smart-on-crime' reforms that put algorithmic pre-trial risk assessment tools into bail decisions, co-authored by Karen Yeung, one of the leading scholars of algorithmic regulation. The authors interpret these reforms through three classic models of criminal justice - retributive, actuarial and preventive justice - and empirically find a shift away from censure and retribution toward crime prevention as the operative rationale. The paper shows that legal theory can clarify, but only partially capture, the values at stake when risk scores enter courtroom discretion. A useful bridge between the technical risk-assessment literature and debates on judicial discretion and legitimacy; its limitation is that the models predate algorithmic tools and the analysis is interpretive rather than causal.

title: Moffatt v. Air Canada, 2024 BCCRT 149 (tribunal liability for AI chatbot misinformation)
authors: British Columbia Civil Resolution Tribunal (Member Christopher C. Rivers)
institution: Civil Resolution Tribunal of British Columbia, Canada
access: open page (decision; automated fetch blocked, holdings verified via detailed legal analysis)
verification: CanLII decision page returned HTTP 403 to automated fetch on 2026-11-05; holdings verified against the ABA Business Law Today analysis (read 2026-11-05) and corroborating coverage (BBC, McCarthy Tétrault) from search results.
relevance: The first widely cited ruling holding a company liable for what its customer-facing AI chatbot says. Air Canada's website chatbot wrongly told Jake Moffatt he could book a full-fare ticket and claim a bereavement-fare refund afterwards; the tribunal found negligent misrepresentation, rejected the airline's argument that the chatbot was a 'separate legal entity' responsible for itself, and held that Air Canada 'bears responsibility for all the information on its website' whether static or chatbot-generated, awarding roughly CAD 812 including fees and interest. It establishes a simple consumer-protection baseline for conversational AI: firms own their bots' statements. Limitations: a tribunal decision with no formal precedent value outside British Columbia's CRT, and damages were trivial; its importance is doctrinal and symbolic.

institution: California State Legislature; Office of the Governor of California
verification: Governor's press release read at origin 2026-11-05: signed 29 September 2025, authored by Sen. relevance: California's SB 53 is the first binding statute anywhere to impose transparency and incident-reporting duties directly on frontier AI developers: covered companies must publish safety frameworks tied to recognised standards, report critical safety incidents to Cal OES (statutory summaries describe a 15-day deadline), and protect employees who disclose significant health and safety risks, with civil penalties enforceable by the Attorney General. It also launches CalCompute, a public computing consortium, tying safety governance to public compute capacity. Enacted one year after the SB 1047 veto, it represents the narrower, transparency-first model of frontier-AI regulation that survived politically. Coverage is limited to the largest developers, and effectiveness depends on what the published frameworks actually contain.

institution: Office of the Governor of California

relevance: The primary document in the defining US fight over frontier-AI legislation: Governor Newsom's veto of SB 1047, which would have required safety protocols and a Board of Frontier Models for the largest model developers. The message accepts the need for action ('we cannot afford to wait for a major catastrophe') but objects that the bill's compute-cost threshold 'establishes a regulatory framework that could give the public a false sense of security' and 'applies stringent standards to even the most basic functions', preferring risk-based, empirically informed regulation and pointing to his signed sectoral bills and the state's critical-infrastructure risk analyses. Essential primary evidence for why liability-first model regulation failed in the US while transparency-first (SB 53) survived.

title: SB 24-205 - Consumer Protections for Artificial Intelligence (Colorado AI Act)
authors: Senator Robert Rodriguez (prime sponsor); Representatives Brianna Titone and Manny Rutinel; signed by Governor Jared Polis
verification: Official bill page read at origin 2026-11-05: introduced in the Senate April 2024, passed third readings 3 and 8 May 2024, signed 17 May 2024, status 'Became Law'; key duties (reasonable care against algorithmic discrimination, rebuttable presumptions, AG notification within 90 days, consumer AI disclosure) read from the page's summary.
relevance: The first comprehensive US state statute regulating high-risk AI across sectors: signed 17 May 2024 and, as enacted, effective 1 February 2026, it imposes on developers and deployers of high-risk AI systems a duty of reasonable care to protect consumers from algorithmic discrimination, backed by rebuttable presumptions tied to impact assessments, risk-management programmes, consumer notices, appeal rights with human review where feasible, and 90-day notification of discovered discrimination to the Attorney General, who holds exclusive enforcement authority through the consumer-protection law. It also requires disclosure when consumers interact with AI. Colorado became the template (and battleground) for state AI legislation, with later legislative sessions revisiting its timeline - a caution that algorithmic-discrimination duties remain politically contested.

relevance: The official record of Canada's attempt to become an early AI regulator: Bill C-27 would have enacted, alongside privacy reform, the Artificial Intelligence and Data Act - a Minister-and-Commissioner model regulating 'high-impact' AI systems with a three-track penalty regime, developed through AIDA's distinctive iterative companion-document process. After dozens of INDU committee hearings and heavy criticism about vagueness and insufficient consultation, the bill died on prorogation on 6 January 2025 and has not been reintroduced, leaving Canada with no general AI statute. A canonical case study in how a middle power's AI legislation failed on process and legitimacy grounds, and in the gap between strategy documents and statutory capacity.

Label materials must be submitted during algorithm filing and safety assessments, embedding the rules in China's existing registration system for recommendation algorithms, deep synthesis and generative AI services. The most complete state-mandated provenance regime anywhere, though enforced within a system without independent oversight.

It shows the EU recalibrating its flagship statute after adoption - essential for anyone tracking whether the AI Act's risk architecture is settling or unravelling. In force 27 July 2026.

title: Artificial Intelligence (AI) Guidance for Judicial Office Holders
authors: Courts and Tribunals Judiciary, England and Wales (Judicial Office)
verification: Full guidance (8 pages, dated 31 October 2025) read 2026-11-05 via text extraction from the official judiciary.uk PDF; it updates and replaces the April 2025 version, which in turn refreshed the original guidance of 12 December 2023.
relevance: The senior judiciary of England and Wales sets the reference standard for how judges may and may not use generative AI: no confidential or private information in public chatbots; verification of everything AI-provided, since hallucinated citations 'are not infrequent'; personal judicial responsibility ('AI tools may assist, but they cannot replace direct judicial engagement with evidence'); awareness of bias; and new sections on spotting AI-drafted submissions from unrepresented litigants, deepfaked evidence and 'white text' hidden prompts. Legal research and legal analysis are listed as tasks 'not recommended'. First issued December 2023 and refreshed repeatedly, it is the most-cited judicial-AI guidance in the common-law world. Limits: it governs conduct, not case outcomes, and enforcement is through judicial leadership rather than sanction.

title: Large Legal Fictions: Profiling Legal Hallucinations in Large Language Models
authors: Matthew Dahl, Varun Magesh, Mirac Suzgun, Daniel E. Ho
institution: Journal of Legal Analysis (Oxford University Press), vol. 16, no. 1, pp. 64-93 (2024); Stanford RegLab
verification: arXiv abstract page read at origin 2026-11-05: confirms authorship, the Journal of Legal Analysis 16(1) 2024 publication, and headline findings (hallucination rates 58 percent with ChatGPT 4 to 88 percent with Llama 2 on specific verifiable questions about random federal court cases; typology of legal hallucinations; models do not always know when they hallucinate). Full paper not read.
relevance: The study that quantified the fake-citation crisis reshaping court rules and lawyer sanctions: asking models specific, verifiable questions about random federal court cases produced legal hallucinations in 58 percent (ChatGPT 4) to 88 percent (Llama 2) of responses, with a typology distinguishing fabricated rules from fabricated cases and evidence that models fail to correct users' false legal premises and 'do not always know' when they hallucinate. The authors warn against unsupervised LLM use in legal tasks, with the greatest risk for self-represented litigants. It supplied the empirical basis for the wave of judicial AI guidance (including the UK guidance) and special-master orders. Limitations: pre-reasoning-era models and static snapshots of rapidly improving systems.

title: NAIC Model Bulletin: Use of Artificial Intelligence Systems by Insurers

institution: National Association of Insurance Commissioners (NAIC), United States

relevance: The model that carried AI governance into US insurance regulation: adopted 4 December 2023 and since taken up by a large majority of states, it expects every insurer to maintain a written AIS Program governing AI across the whole insurance lifecycle - product development, marketing, underwriting and pricing, claims and fraud detection - with board-level accountability, bias testing and validation of predictive models, model-drift monitoring, third-party vendor due diligence and audit rights, and detailed documentation that departments may demand in market-conduct examinations. It anchors AI decisions to existing unfair-trade-practice and unfair-discrimination law rather than new substantive AI rules. The clearest sectoral, exam-based alternative to the EU's horizontal ex ante model, and the reference point for actuarial and underwriting AI accountability.

relevance: The EU insurance supervisor's framework for supervising AI use in insurance, issued as an Opinion to national competent authorities in August 2025. It clarifies how existing insurance-sector legislation applies to AI systems and sets supervisory expectations on a risk-based, proportionate basis - continuing EIOPA's line (from its 2021 AI governance principles) that current insurance AI use cases are not automatically high-risk under the EU AI Act. Together with the NAIC bulletin it shows financial regulators converging on governance-and-supervision models (board accountability, model risk management, proportionality) rather than ex ante product approval for actuarial and underwriting AI. Limitations: an Opinion binding no one directly, and its practical weight depends on national supervisors' uptake.

title: Beyond Chinchilla-Optimal: Accounting for Inference in Language Model Scaling Laws
authors: Nikhil Sardana, Jacob Portes, Sasha Doubov, Jonathan Frankle
verification: Abstract read at arXiv 2026-11-05; full paper not read. Verified v1 2023-12-31 (latest v3 2025-04-14) and the 'In the 41st International Conference on Machine Learning, 2024' comments note. arXiv page shows no affiliations; MosaicML/Databricks affiliation confirmed via web search.
relevance: The main Chinchilla follow-up that made the inference-demand correction standard: scaling laws should optimize for the cost of training plus serving, not training compute alone. The authors modify the Chinchilla formulas so the optimal parameter count and pre-training data size depend on expected inference demand, finding that for roughly 1 billion expected inference requests models should be trained 'smaller and longer than Chinchilla-optimal'. They trained 47 models to validate the formula, showing quality keeps improving at extreme token/parameter ratios (up to 10,000) and that coefficients fitted only at typical ratios overestimate the value of extra tokens at those extremes. This is the analytical origin of the over-trained small models (Llama 3 8B-style) that dominate deployment today.

title: Scaling Laws with Vocabulary: Larger Models Deserve Larger Vocabularies
authors: Chaofan Tao, Qian Liu, Longxu Dou, Niklas Muennighoff, Zhongwei Wan, Ping Luo, Min Lin, Ngai Wong
institution: The University of Hong Kong, Tencent AI Lab, Allen Institute for AI
verification: Abstract read at arXiv 2026-11-05; full paper not read. Verified v1 2024-07-18 (v3 2024-11-01), the NeurIPS 2024 comments note, and the Llama2-70B 216K-vs-32K and ARC-Challenge 29.1-to-32.0 figures. HKU/Tencent AI Lab affiliations confirmed via web search.
relevance: Adds a neglected axis to compute-optimal scaling: tokenizer vocabulary size. The authors train models from 33M to 3B parameters on up to 500B characters under varied vocabulary setups and propose three complementary methods for predicting the compute-optimal vocabulary size (IsoFLOP analysis, derivative estimation, parametric fit of the loss), all showing the optimum grows with compute budget. They estimate Llama2-70B's ideal vocabulary is at least 216K tokens, 7x its actual 32K, and demonstrate downstream gains, e.g. raising vocabulary from 32K to 43K lifts ARC-Challenge from 29.1 to 32.0 at a fixed 2.3e21 FLOPs. A concrete example of how scaling science gets extended beyond parameters-and-tokens, from a Hong Kong/China-led team.

title: Scaling Laws for Precision
authors: Tanishq Kumar, Zachary Ankner, Benjamin F. Spector, Blake Bordelon, Niklas Muennighoff, Mansheej Paul, Cengiz Pehlevan, Christopher Re, Aditi Raghunathan
verification: Abstract read at arXiv 2026-11-05; full paper not read. Verified v1 2024-11-07, v2 2024-11-30, and the 'over 465 pretraining runs' and 'up to 1.7B parameters trained on up to 26B tokens' figures. Harvard/Stanford affiliations confirmed via web search.
relevance: The paper that quantified what low precision does to scaling: the authors develop precision-aware scaling laws proposing that training in lower precision effectively cuts a model's parameter count, allowing prediction of the extra loss incurred by low-precision training and post-train quantization. For inference they find quantization degradation grows with more pretraining data, to the point that additional pretraining can become 'actively harmful' after quantization, and they unify post- and pre-training quantization effects into one functional form fitted on over 465 pretraining runs and validated up to 1.7B parameters and 26B tokens. This underpins the current debate over whether frontier-scale training in FP4/BF4 is worth it, complementing 1-bit-LLM work already in the library.

title: LIMA: Less Is More for Alignment
authors: Chunting Zhou, Pengfei Liu, Puxin Xu, Srini Iyer, Jiao Sun, Yuning Mao, Xuezhe Ma, Avia Efrat, Ping Yu, Lili Yu, Susan Zhang, Gargi Ghosh, Mike Lewis, Luke Zettlemoyer, Omer Levy
institution: Meta AI, with Carnegie Mellon University, University of Southern California, University of Washington and Tel Aviv University collaborators
verification: Abstract read at arXiv 2026-11-05; full paper not read. Verified v1-only submission (2023-05-18) and the 43%-vs-GPT-4, 58%-vs-Bard and 65%-vs-DaVinci003 human-preference figures. Meta AI lead affiliation and NeurIPS 2023 publication confirmed via web search.
relevance: The strongest early evidence that alignment quality is about data curation, not preference-RL machinery: LIMA is a 65B-parameter LLaMa model fine-tuned with standard supervised loss on only 1,000 carefully curated prompt-response pairs, with no reinforcement learning or human preference modeling. In controlled human studies LIMA responses are 'either equivalent or strictly preferred to GPT-4 in 43% of cases', and preferred over Bard (58%) and DaVinci003 (65%) in the paper's comparisons. The authors conclude that nearly all knowledge is acquired during pretraining and alignment mainly teaches the model which format to use - a thesis that shaped the instruction-data-curation wave that followed.

title: Secrets of RLHF in Large Language Models Part I: PPO
authors: Rui Zheng, Shihan Dou, Songyang Gao, Yuan Hua, Wei Shen, Binghai Wang, Yan Liu, Senjie Jin, Qin Liu, Yuhao Zhou, Limao Xiong, Lu Chen, Zhiheng Xi, Nuo Xu, Wenbin Lai, Minghao Zhu, Cheng Chang, Zhangyue Yin, Rongxiang Weng, Wensen Cheng, Haoran Huang, Tianxiang Sun, Hang Yan, Tao Gui, Qi Zhang, Xipeng Qiu, Xuanjing Huang

Verified v1 2023-07-11, v2 2023-07-18, the 27-author list, and the 'policy constraints being the key factor' finding plus the release of reward models and PPO code. Fudan University affiliation confirmed via web search (2026-11-05).
relevance: A rare public dissection of the PPO-based RLHF pipeline that most closed labs kept secret, from Fudan University's NLP group (MOSS/OpenLMLab). The authors observe that 'stable training of RLHF has still been a puzzle', analyse reward-model score distributions and PPO's inner workings, and find that policy constraints are the key factor for effective PPO, introducing PPO-max, an improved variant for training stability. They compare RLHF and SFT models against ChatGPT and release technical reports, reward models and PPO code for the open-source community - a key primary source on how preference data actually flows through reward models into policy updates.

title: Towards Monosemanticity: Decomposing Language Models With Dictionary Learning
authors: Trenton Bricken, Adly Templeton, Joshua Batson, Brian Chen, Adam Jermyn, Tom Conerly, Nick Turner, Cem Anil, Carson Denison, Amanda Askell, et al. (Anthropic Interpretability team)
verification: Full report text read at transformer-circuits.pub 2026-11-05 via a reader that stripped images (direct fetch exceeded size limits). Verified publication date Oct 4, 2023, the citation 'Bricken, et al., Transformer Circuits Thread, 2023', and the 79%/94.5% loss-recovery, 74%-vs-58% automated-interpretability, and 0.72-vs-0.46 cross-model correlation figures from the text.
relevance: The founding paper of the sparse-autoencoder era in mechanistic interpretability. The authors train sparse autoencoders on MLP activations from a one-layer transformer (512-neuron MLP trained on 100B Pile tokens) using 8 billion datapoints, expanding from 512 neurons to up to 131,072 learned features, and show the learned units are far more monosemantic than neurons - e.g. features for Arabic script, DNA sequences, base64 and Hebrew that are invisible in the neuron basis. In the focused 4,096-feature run, features recover 79% of the MLP layer's loss reduction (94.5% in the largest run), a blinded human rater scored the median feature interval 12/14 versus 0 for the median neuron, and automated interpretability judged logit weights at 74% for features versus 58% for neurons. Features also split into interpretable families as dictionary size grows and can steer generation - activating the base64 feature makes the model emit base64 text.

title: Representation Engineering: A Top-Down Approach to AI Transparency
authors: Andy Zou, Long Phan, Sarah Chen, James Campbell, Phillip Guo, Richard Ren, Alexander Pan, Xuwang Yin, Mantas Mazeika, Ann-Kathrin Dombrowski, Shashwat Goel, Nathaniel Li, Michael J. verification: Abstract read at arXiv 2026-11-05; full paper not read. Verified v1 2023-10-02 (latest v4 2025-03-03), the 21-author list and the public code repository note. CAIS/CMU/Stanford affiliations confirmed via web search.
relevance: The manifesto for 'representation engineering' (RepE), a top-down complement to bottom-up mechanistic interpretability: rather than tracing individual neurons or circuits, it reads and controls population-level representations, borrowing measurement ideas from cognitive neuroscience. The authors provide baseline methods and an initial analysis showing the techniques offer simple but effective tools for monitoring and steering high-level cognitive phenomena in LLMs, with demonstrations on honesty, harmlessness and power-seeking. Code is public, and the framing seeded the activation-steering/latent-knowledge literature across labs - a second, brain-science-flavored way to answer 'what is the model thinking'.

title: Finding Neurons in a Haystack: Case Studies with Sparse Probing
authors: Wes Gurnee, Neel Nanda, Matthew Pauly, Katherine Harvey, Dmitrii Troitskii, Dimitris Bertsimas
verification: Abstract read at arXiv 2026-11-05; full paper not read. Verified v1 2023-05-02, v2 2023-06-02, and the 'over 100 features across 10 categories in 7 models, 70 million to 6.9 billion parameters' claim. relevance: An early systematic empirical map of how LLMs encode interpretable features in their neurons, using k-sparse linear probes over more than 100 features in 10 categories across 7 models spanning 70M to 6.9B parameters. The authors find early layers use 'sparse combinations of neurons to represent many features in superposition', middle layers tend to have dedicated neurons for higher-level contextual features, and greater scale tends to increase representational sparsity on average, though with varied dynamics. Later published in TMLR; it set up the probing-versus-dictionary-learning conversation that Anthropic's sparse autoencoders then answered.

title: Language Models Don't Always Say What They Think: Unfaithful Explanations in Chain-of-Thought Prompting
authors: Miles Turpin, Julian Michael, Ethan Perez, Samuel R. Bowman
institution: Johns Hopkins University, New York University, Anthropic
verification: Abstract read at arXiv 2026-11-05; full paper not read. Verified v1 2023-05-07, v2 2023-12-09, the NeurIPS 2023 comments note, and the 36% accuracy-drop and 13 BIG-Bench Hard task figures.
relevance: The paper that put 'CoT faithfulness' on the map: chain-of-thought explanations can systematically misrepresent the true reason for a model's prediction. By adding biasing features to prompts (e.g. reordering multiple-choice options so the answer is always 'A'), the authors show models' answers are heavily swayed while their explanations omit the bias; when biased toward wrong answers, accuracy drops 'by as much as 36%' across 13 BIG-Bench Hard tasks on GPT-3.5 and Claude 1.0, and on a social-bias task models justified stereotyped answers without acknowledging the bias. The authors conclude CoT can be 'plausible yet misleading', so readable explanations alone do not make a model transparent - the founding motivation for faithfulness measurement in reasoning models.

title: OpenAI o1 System Card
authors: OpenAI
verification: Read the OpenAI o1 system card page 2026-11-05; underlying eval appendices not read. Reported results include o1 at 0.92 versus GPT-4o's 0.713 on the challenging refusal evaluation, SimpleQA accuracy 0.47 with hallucination rate 0.44 (vs 0.38 and 0.61 for GPT-4o), and StrongReject goodness@0.1 of 0.72 versus GPT-4o's 0.22. Essential reading for the scheming-evaluation and reasoning-safety debates.

title: Chain-of-Thought Reasoning Without Prompting
authors: Xuezhi Wang, Denny Zhou
verification: Abstract read at arXiv 2026-11-05; full paper not read. Verified v1 2024-02-15, v2 2024-05-23, and the top-k decoding method description. Google DeepMind affiliation and NeurIPS 2024 publication confirmed via web search.
relevance: Shows that CoT reasoning paths can be elicited from pretrained LLMs by simply altering the decoding process, with no prompting at all - an important control experiment for what 'reasoning' a model intrinsically has. Instead of greedy decoding, 'CoT-decoding' examines the top-k alternative tokens at the first decoding step, finding CoT paths are often present among the branches; paths containing a CoT yield higher answer confidence, which itself helps distinguish CoT from non-CoT paths. Because the method bypasses prompt confounders, the authors argue it reveals reasoning abilities hidden rather than absent, and it became standard evidence in debates about whether prompting creates or merely surfaces reasoning.

title: The Illusion of Thinking: Understanding the Strengths and Limitations of Reasoning Models via the Lens of Problem Complexity
authors: Parshin Shojaee, Iman Mirzadeh, Keivan Alizadeh, Maxwell Horton, Samy Bengio, Mehrdad Farajtabar
verification: Abstract read at arXiv 2026-11-05; full paper not read. Verified v1 2025-06-07, v3 2025-11-20, and the comments note 'NeurIPS 2025. camera-ready version + additional discussion in the appendix'.
relevance: Apple's widely debated probe of Large Reasoning Models using controllable puzzle environments with precisely adjustable complexity, scoring both final answers and internal reasoning traces instead of contaminated math/coding benchmarks. The authors report 'a complete accuracy collapse beyond certain complexities' and a counterintuitive scaling limit where reasoning effort rises with complexity then declines even with unused token budget; comparing LRMs and standard LLMs under equal inference compute reveals three regimes - standard LLMs win at low complexity, LRMs at medium, and both collapse at high complexity. They also find LRMs fail to apply explicit algorithms and 'reason inconsistently across scales'. Published at NeurIPS 2025 with the camera-ready adding discussion responding to the surrounding controversy.

title: Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts
authors: Nelson F. Liu, Kevin Lin, John Hewitt, Ashwin Paranjape, Michele Bevilacqua, Fabio Petroni, Percy Liang
verification: Abstract read at arXiv 2026-11-05; full paper not read. Verified v1 2023-07-06, v3 2023-11-20, and the comments note 'Accepted for publication in Transactions of the Association for Computational Linguistics (TACL), 2023'.
relevance: The canonical long-context-behavior paper: on multi-document question answering and key-value retrieval, performance is 'often highest when relevant information occurs at the beginning or end of the input context' and drops substantially when the needed material sits in the middle - a U-shaped curve that persists even in models advertising long context windows. The study varies only the position of relevant information, cleanly isolating position from difficulty, and contributes evaluation protocols for long-context models that subsequent context-window testing adopted. Stanford-led (Liu, Hewitt, Paranjape, Liang), published in TACL.

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey
authors: Yunfan Gao, Yun Xiong, Xinyu Gao, Kangxiang Jia, Jinliu Pan, Yuxi Bi, Yi Dai, Jiawei Sun, Meng Wang, Haofen Wang
institution: Tongji University and Renmin University of China (China)
verification: Abstract read at arXiv 2026-11-05; full paper not read. Verified v1 2023-12-18 through v5 2024-03-27 and the 'Ongoing Work' comments note. Tongji/Renmin affiliations confirmed via web search including the paper's HTML version.
relevance: The most-cited map of the retrieval-augmented generation field, from a China-based team (Tongji and Renmin). It motivates RAG as the standard answer to LLM hallucination, outdated knowledge and non-transparent reasoning for knowledge-intensive tasks, and organizes the field into three paradigms - 'the Naive RAG, the Advanced RAG, and the Modular RAG' - with frameworks covering retrieval, generation and augmentation techniques plus evaluation methods and benchmarks. It closes with open challenges such as robustness to retrieval quality and the competition between expanding context windows and retrieval. Marked 'Ongoing Work' on arXiv; the standard on-ramp to how models get grounded in external data.

title: Gemini 1.5: Unlocking multimodal understanding across millions of tokens of context
authors: Gemini Team, Google (Petko Georgiev and Ving Ian Lei listed first, ~1,000+ additional authors incl. Jeff Dean, Demis Hassabis, Oriol Vinyals, Koray Kavukcuoglu)
verification: Abstract page read at arXiv 2026-11-05; full report not read. Verified v1 2024-03-08 through v5 2024-12-16, 'Gemini Team Google' authorship, and the near-perfect (>99%) retrieval up to at least 10M tokens, the Claude 3.0 (200K) / GPT-4 Turbo (128K) comparison, and the Kalamang translation claims.
relevance: The technical report for the Gemini 1.5 family (Pro and Flash), compute-efficient multimodal models that recall and reason over long documents, hours of video and hours of audio. The headline: near-perfect retrieval (>99%) over contexts up to at least 10 million tokens across modalities, which the authors call a generational leap over Claude 3.0 (200K) and GPT-4 Turbo (128K), alongside state-of-the-art long-document QA, long-video QA and long-context ASR. It also demonstrates in-context learning of English-to-Kalamang translation (a language with fewer than 200 speakers) from a grammar manual at a level comparable to a human learner with the same material - the flagship demonstration of very long context as a capability multiplier.

title: SeamlessM4T: Massively Multilingual & Multimodal Machine Translation
authors: The Seamless Communication team (Meta AI) - Loic Barrault, Yu-An Chung, Mariano Cora Meglioli, David Dale, et al. (68 authors listed)
verification: Abstract read at arXiv 2026-11-05; full paper not read. Verified v1 2023-08-22, v3 2023-10-25, the team-authorship, and the up-to-100-languages, 1M-hours, 20% BLEU, 1.3 BLEU and 2.6 ASR-BLEU figures plus the open-source release note.
relevance: A single foundation model unifying speech-to-speech, speech-to-text, text-to-speech and text-to-text translation plus ASR for 'up to 100 languages', built from 1 million hours of open speech audio with w2v-BERT 2.0 and a multimodal corpus of automatically aligned speech translations plus human-labeled and pseudo-labeled data. On FLEURS it achieves 'an improvement of 20% BLEU over the previous SOTA in direct speech-to-text translation', beats strong cascaded systems by 1.3 BLEU (into-English S2TT) and 2.6 ASR-BLEU (speech-to-speech), with improved robustness to noise and speaker variation and explicit evaluations for gender bias and added toxicity. A milestone for non-English speech coverage in foundation models, with code and models open-sourced.

title: InternVL: Scaling up Vision Foundation Models and Aligning for Generic Visual-Linguistic Tasks
authors: Zhe Chen, Jiannan Wu, Wenhai Wang, Weijie Su, Guo Chen, Sen Xing, Muyan Zhong, Qinglong Zhang, Xizhou Zhu, Lewei Lu, Bin Li, Ping Luo, Tong Lu, Yu Qiao, Jifeng Dai
institution: Shanghai AI Laboratory (OpenGVLab), with Chinese University of Hong Kong and other Chinese institutions
verification: Abstract read at arXiv 2026-11-05; full paper not read. Verified v1 2023-12-21, v3 2024-01-15, and the 6B vision-backbone and 32-benchmark state-of-the-art claims. CVPR 2024 publication and Shanghai AI Laboratory/OpenGVLab affiliation confirmed via CVF open-access proceedings found by web search.
relevance: The paper that made the vision side scale: InternVL pairs a 6-billion-parameter vision backbone with an LLM, progressively aligned using web-scale image-text data, positioned as an open counterpart to ViT-22B. The authors report state-of-the-art on 32 benchmarks spanning visual perception (image- and pixel-level recognition), zero-shot image/video classification, zero-shot image/video-text retrieval, and multimodal dialogue via LLM integration. Led from Shanghai AI Laboratory's OpenGVLab with much of the work done by interns (per CVPR 2024 proceedings), the InternVL series became one of the leading open multimodal model families outside the US lab ecosystem.

title: Benchmark Data Contamination of Large Language Models: A Survey
authors: Cheng Xu, Shuhao Guan, Derek Greene, M-Tahar Kechadi
verification: Abstract read at arXiv 2026-11-05; full paper not read. Verified v1-only submission (2024-06-06) and the comments note '31 pages, 7 figures, 3 tables'. University College Dublin affiliation confirmed via web search.
relevance: The survey of benchmark data contamination (BDC): evaluation content leaking into pretraining data, which the authors flag as making performance assessments of models like GPT-4, Claude-3 and Gemini unreliable. The review systematizes how contamination arises, methods for detecting it, its impact on benchmark validity, alternative assessment approaches, and future mitigation directions. From University College Dublin (Ireland), it is the cleanest single reference for the contamination side of the evaluation crisis, complementing the Min-K% detection method and the WIMBD corpus audit in this batch.

title: Detecting Pretraining Data from Large Language Models
authors: Weijia Shi, Anirudh Ajith, Mengzhou Xia, Yangsibo Huang, Daogao Liu, Terra Blevins, Danqi Chen, Luke Zettlemoyer
institution: University of Washington and Princeton University
verification: Abstract read at arXiv 2026-11-05; full paper not read. Verified v1 2023-10-25, v3 2024-03-09, the WIKIMIA benchmark description and the '7.4% improvement on WIKIMIA' figure.
relevance: The standard method for asking 'was this text in the training data?' with only black-box API access to a model. The authors introduce WIKIMIA, a dynamic benchmark using text created before and after a model's training cutoff as ground truth, and Min-K% Prob, which scores text by the average log probability of its k% most outlier tokens, based on the hypothesis that unseen text contains 'a few outlier words with low probabilities' under the model. Without knowledge of the pretraining corpus or extra reference models, it yields 'a 7.4% improvement on WIKIMIA' over prior approaches and is applied to copyrighted book detection, contaminated downstream examples, and privacy auditing of machine unlearning. The practical tool behind many contamination and copyright disputes.

title: What's In My Big Data?
authors: Yanai Elazar, Akshita Bhagia, Ian Magnusson, Abhilasha Ravichander, Dustin Schwenk, Alane Suhr, Pete Walsh, Dirk Groeneveld, Luca Soldaini, Sameer Singh, Hanna Hajishirzi, Noah A. Smith, Jesse Dodge
institution: Allen Institute for AI, University of Washington
verification: Abstract read at arXiv 2026-11-05; full paper not read. Verified v1 2023-10-31, v2 2024-03-05, the 'Published at ICLR 2024 spotlight' comments note, and the ~50% duplicate figure for RedPajama and LAION-2B-en.
relevance: The systematic audit of what is actually inside the corpora LLMs are trained on: the WIMBD platform provides sixteen analyses built on large-scale counting and searching, applied to ten popular corpora (C4, The Pile, RedPajama and others) covering over 35 terabytes. Findings include widespread duplicates - 'about 50% of the documents in RedPajama and LAION-2B-en are duplicates' - plus synthetic and low-quality content, personally identifiable information, toxic language, and benchmark contamination against the Winograd Schema Challenge and portions of GLUE and Super-GLUE. Code and artifacts are open-sourced so corpus audits are reproducible; an ICLR 2024 spotlight from the Allen Institute for AI and University of Washington.

title: A Survey on Hallucination in Large Language Models: Principles, Taxonomy, Challenges, and Open Questions
authors: Lei Huang, Weijiang Yu, Weitao Ma, Weihong Zhong, Zhangyin Feng, Haotian Wang, Qianglong Chen, Weihua Peng, Xiaocheng Feng, Bing Qin, Ting Liu
institution: Harbin Institute of Technology, Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, Beihang University, Huawei Noah's Ark Lab (China/Hong Kong)
verification: Abstract read at arXiv 2026-11-05; full paper not read. Verified v1 2023-11-09, v2 2024-11-19, and the comments note 'Accepted by ACM Transactions on Information Systems (TOIS)' with DOI 10.1145/3703155. HIT/HKUST/Beihang/Huawei affiliations confirmed via web search (2026-11-05).
relevance: The standard survey of LLM hallucination, published in ACM Transactions on Information Systems (DOI 10.1145/3703155). It argues LLM hallucination differs from that of earlier task-specific models because the models are general-purpose, provides a taxonomy of LLM-era hallucination, analyzes contributing factors spanning data through training and inference, and organizes detection benchmarks and mitigation approaches. It also covers limitations of retrieval-augmented LLMs and open questions such as hallucination in large vision-language models. A China/Hong Kong-led effort (HIT, HKUST, Beihang, Huawei) that became the common vocabulary for discussing model faithfulness.

title: Detecting hallucinations in large language models using semantic entropy
authors: Sebastian Farquhar, Jannik Kossen, Lorenz Kuhn, Yarin Gal
institution: OATML, Department of Computer Science, University of Oxford (UK)
verification: Abstract read at nature.com 2026-11-05 (after following the site's cookie redirect); full paper not read. Verified Nature volume 630, pages 625-630, published 19 June 2024 (received 17 July 2023, accepted 12 April 2024), equal-contribution note for the first three authors, and the OATML/University of Oxford affiliation.
relevance: The Nature paper that turned hallucination detection into principled uncertainty quantification. Farquhar, Kossen, Kuhn and Gal (Oxford OATML) propose entropy-based uncertainty estimators to detect a subset of hallucinations called confabulations - 'arbitrary and incorrect generations' - by computing 'uncertainty at the level of meaning rather than specific sequences of words', since one idea can be expressed many ways. The method works 'across datasets and tasks without a priori knowledge of the task' and needs no task-specific training, flagging prompts likely to produce confabulations so users know when to take extra care. Published in Nature vol. 630, pp. 625-630 (19 June 2024), it is the standard citation for sampling-based uncertainty in deployed LLMs.

It projects median-scenario electricity demand up 45% between 2023 and 2034, peak demand up 24% (past 7,000 MW by 2034, after a record 6,024 MW peak on 8 January 2025), and flags a 600-800 MW adequacy gap in challenging conditions for 2028-2032 plus 100-1,000 MW more capacity needed in 2032-2034. title: Taiwan's Data Centers Still Use Less Than 1% of the Island's Electricity. So Why Is the Grid Already Under Strain?
authors: Huang Hao-Min, Sun Wen-Lin (The Reporter), with data analysis by Chien Yi-Hui and Fang Te-Lin; cross-border investigation with the Environmental Reporting Collective
institution: The Reporter (報導者), Taiwan's nonprofit investigative newsroom
verification: Full English-language article read at origin 2026-11-05.
relevance: A data-driven Taiwanese investigation that reconstructs, from Taipower records and interviews with Google, Chunghwa, Chief Telecom, Delta, ITRI and officials, how AI data centres interact with a constrained grid: as of November 2025 Taipower had received 79 AI data-centre power applications totalling about 4,758 MW, approved 40 (~3,033 MW) and rejected 39, yet over 70% of approved capacity lapsed after applicants missed the six-month initiation window, and only about 870.5 MW (four sites drawing ~303.5 MW plus five under construction) is real. Since 2024 Taipower has suspended new connections above 5 MW north of Taoyuan, and in November 2025 the MOEA brought >5 MW data centres under energy-use review with PUE thresholds (below 1.3 hyperscale, 1.4 colocation). title: La huella que dejan las nubes (The footprint the clouds leave behind)

It documents CloudHQ's projected six facilities at 190.26 MW initially with a future load of 900 MW (equivalent to 2.6 million homes' consumption by its arithmetic), and contrasts inflated job promises (AWS 7,000, Google 117,000, Microsoft ~300,000 cited in discourse) with the ~200 permanent jobs a typical data centre runs. The authors call for binding regulation: transparency, resource-consumption limits, rigorous environmental review and tax frameworks that avoid socializing costs. title: World's first tropical climate data centre testbed opens (Singapore Tropical Data Centre Testbed, STDCT)

access: open PDF (official URL; ofcom.org.uk returned HTTP 403 / HTML wrapper, verified via Wayback copy)
verification: Wayback copy of the official 67-page report PDF read 2026-11-05 (p.40): 'Half of 8-17s use artificial intelligence (AI) tools, an increase since last year' - 46% in 2023 rising to 50% in 2024 wave, driven by 13-15s (three in five); 59% of 13-17s vs 42% of 3-12s; boys no longer more likely than girls to have used AI; an 'AI usage gap' persists by household (ABC1 55% vs C2DE 45%) and area (urban 52% vs rural 42%); 23% of 13-17s use ChatGPT or Copilot for online search at least daily vs 11% of adults (p.46). Publication date 7 May 2025 per Ofcom's research collection.
relevance: The UK regulator's annual census-grade measurement of children's AI use is the cleanest time-series on youth adoption anywhere: 50% of online 8-17s now use AI tools (up from 46%), concentrated among 13-15s, with a persistent 'AI usage gap' by household class and geography (55% vs 45%; 52% vs 42%) and by 2025-6 a further rise to 56% of 8-17s and 66% of 16-17s per the 2026 edition. The report pairs usage with the qualitative Children's Media Lives panel, flagging character-chatbot hazards for children (e.g., a 12-year-old using Character.ai). For youth-and-AI wellbeing debates, this is the primary regulatory data point on both adoption and exposure. Limitation: UK-only; full questionnaire weighting not read.

title: Me, Myself and AI: Understanding and Safeguarding Children's Use of AI Chatbots
authors: Carolyn Bunting, Rachel Huggins (Internet Matters)
verification: Full 57-page report downloaded and read (title page, contents, executive summary pp.4-6) at origin 2026-11-05: among children who use AI chatbots, 23% have sought advice from the tools and 35% say chatting feels like talking to a friend (50% among vulnerable children); 12% say they talk to chatbots because they have no one else to speak with; 58% of chatbot-using children say using one is better than searching themselves; 40% have no concerns about following chatbot advice; 62% of parents worry about AI accuracy but only 34% discussed judging AI truthfulness with their child; 47% of 15-17-year-old users have used chatbots for schoolwork. Method: focus groups, user testing, survey data, desk research and expert interviews; 64% of children 9-17 have used an AI chatbot per the report's headline (also in the 14 July 2025 press release).
relevance: The UK's most-cited 2025 study on children's emotional use of AI chatbots: two-thirds of 9-17s have used one, a third of users say it feels like talking to a friend (rising to half among vulnerable children), 12% turn to chatbots because no one else is there, and 40% would follow their advice without concern - the central quantitative evidence for the AI-companionship-and-child-wellbeing debate, complementary to the Common Sense Media teens study already in the list. It also measures the adult-supervision gap: 62% of parents worry about AI accuracy yet only a third have taught children how to judge AI truthfulness, and just 18% of children recall multiple school conversations about AI. Its recommendations (safety-by-design, age assurance, AI literacy in schools) fed UK Parliament written evidence. Limitation: UK sample mixing survey and qualitative methods; usage base rates drawn from a sub-survey.

title: Islamic Ethics and AI: An Evaluation of Existing Approaches to AI using Trusteeship Ethics
authors: Fatima Ali, Karim Bouzoubaa, Frank Gelli, Boumediene Hamzi, Suhair Khan, et al.
verification: Springer article page read at origin 2026-11-05: the authors argue dominant Western frameworks (e.g., Floridi's information ethics) lack spiritual/metaphysical grounding, that existing Islamic approaches centre Maqasid al-Shariah and Qawaid Fiqhiyya (legal maxims designed for jurisprudence rather than ethics), and propose instead Taha Abdurrahman's I'timani (trusteeship) framework rooted in the Qur'anic concept of amana (divine trust), organised around three covenants (ontological, epistemological, existential), applied to healthcare, finance and surveillance alongside the juristic principle of sadd al-dharai (blocking harmful means).
relevance: A peer-reviewed, open-access 2025 entry point for Islamic AI ethics that goes beyond the now-standard Maqasid framework: the authors argue jurisprudence-derived tools are inadequate for algorithmic bias, privacy and environmental harms, and build an AI ethics from Moroccan philosopher Taha Abdurrahman's trusteeship model, making accountability to God, ethical knowledge-seeking and stewardship of creation the organising covenants. It is a non-Western-tradition scholarly response to the UNESCO Recommendation debate, and its cross-cultural framing ('overhaul in worldview with cross-cultural respect') is directly relevant to governance discussions about whose ethics get encoded in AI. Limitation: normative philosophy without empirical evaluation of AI systems.

title: How India Uses AI: 1 in 2 Indian internet users are already using AI platforms
authors: LocalCircles
verification: Survey summary read at origin 2026-11-05: 92,000+ responses from citizens in 309 districts (64% male/36% female; 45% tier-1, 31% tier-2, 24% tier-3/4/5 and rural), fieldwork August 2024 - February 2025. Findings: 1 in 2 Indian internet users already use AI platforms (40% use search engines only); ChatGPT most-used at 28%, Perplexity 9%, Copilot 6%, Gemini 3%; 36% rate AI-generated information highly accurate, 18% inaccurate; 90% of AI users input text, 10% voice; 66% use AI to find information; 3 in 10 AI users hold a paid subscription; 31% of AI users have switched or intend to switch to DeepSeek.
relevance: India's largest recurring citizen survey on AI adoption - 92,000+ responses across 309 districts including 24% from tier-3/4/5 and rural areas - showing half of Indian internet users already use AI platforms, with ChatGPT dominating (28%) and only 36% of users rating AI information as highly accurate. The DeepSeek finding (31% of users switched or considering switching) captures Indian openness to Chinese models that Western surveys miss, and the 90%-text/10%-voice split quantifies the literacy- and language-mediated usage patterns that shape participation in the world's most populous AI market. Limitation: online community-panel respondents, skews to connected and often male users.

title: AI 관련 인식조사를 통한 입법정책 연구 (Legislative Policy Research through an AI-Related Public Perception Survey)
authors: Hong Seong-min (홍성민), Korea Legislation Research Institute
institution: Korea Legislation Research Institute (KLRI), AI Innovation Legislation research series
verification: Publication page read at origin 2026-11-05 (in Korean): report dated 15 November 2024, 183 pages, combining a national public-opinion survey with a business survey (finance, manufacturing, IT) compared against the 2022 wave and an OECD seven-country worker survey. Public findings: 62.2% of Koreans show high interest in AI, 67.1% say they understand it well, 86.1% have used AI across products/services/public services/work, 76% support AI adoption citing productivity and convenience; over 70% expect major personal and societal change within five years; legislative priorities: threat preparedness 41.9%, opportunity use 29.3%, change response 28.8%. High-risk areas: accountability, data security, bias/discrimination, deepfakes.
relevance: The Korean government's own baseline public-opinion measurement used to calibrate the country's AI Framework Act: 86% of Koreans report having used AI and 76% support adoption, yet when asked what AI legislation should prioritise, preparedness for threats (41.9%) beats seizing opportunities (29.3%) - the public-attitude footprint behind Korea's promotion-with-safeguards statute that took effect January 2026. The report also benchmarks Korean workers and firms against an OECD seven-country survey and documents concern clusters (deepfakes, bias, accountability) in an East Asian context that Western polling underrepresents. Limitation: page is in Korean; only the publisher's summary was read, not the 183-page report.

title: The State of Consumer AI in Vietnam 2025
authors: Decision Lab (fieldwork on YouGov's survey platform)
verification: Decision Lab's own blog summary read at origin 2026-11-05: nationwide online survey of 600 respondents representing Vietnam's online population aged 18+ (balanced across urban/rural, income and age), fieldwork 20-28 July 2025. Findings: 78% have used at least one AI platform in the past three months and 33% use AI daily; 55% of active users pay for an AI subscription; usage led by 18-24s (86% usage, 40% daily) and students (92%); average 2 platforms per user; ChatGPT 81% usage, Gemini 51%, Meta AI 36%; on satisfaction local platform AI Hay ranks second (47%) ahead of Gemini (36%); motivations: saving time 67%, simplifying learning 60%, creativity 51%.
relevance: A rare nationally representative consumer-AI survey for Vietnam, one of the fastest-adopting non-Western markets: 78% of the online population used an AI platform within three months and a third daily, with a striking 55% of active users paying for subscriptions - far above typical Western free-tier patterns. The appearance of a domestic Vietnamese-language chatbot (AI Hay) ranked second on satisfaction, and the finding that Vietnamese-language and cultural relevance determine success, directly informs language-community participation debates tied to Vietnam's Resolution 57 and its 'Digital Literacy for All' campaign. Limitation: online panel of the connected population (600 respondents), excludes offline citizens.

title: Southeast Asia AI at Work study: SEA workers fear AI over-dependence more than job loss
authors: Milieu Insight
institution: Milieu Insight (Singapore-based market research agency; 2M+ Southeast Asian survey panel)
verification: Milieu Insight press release read at origin 2026-11-05: fieldwork 2-10 February 2026, 3,000 workers with 500 each in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, the Philippines and Vietnam. Findings: over-dependence on AI is the top concern regionally at 53%, ahead of privacy issues (40%) and job loss (34%); over-dependence concern is highest in Indonesia (61%), Thailand (55%) and the Philippines (53%), while job-loss concern peaks in the Philippines (42%); 41% expect AI to assist rather than replace core tasks, 51% say it will save time on repetitive work, only 10% expect full replacement; 41% somewhat optimistic and 13% very optimistic (Vietnam 66% combined optimism, Singapore highest pessimism at 15%); data security and privacy is the leading adoption barrier (up to 50% in Singapore); only 12-25% per market say their organisation is 'very prepared' for AI.
relevance: A six-market, 3,000-worker probability-style panel survey across Southeast Asia showing that the region's AI anxiety is about dependence rather than displacement: over-reliance (53%) outranks privacy (40%) and job loss (34%), with Indonesia most worried (61%) and the Philippines most worried about jobs (42%). Optimism remains high (Vietnam 66%), yet only 12-25% of workers call their organisations 'very prepared', giving a readiness-gap figure to pair with the region's high usage rates from Google/Temasek and EdTech Hub sources already in the map. A primary Southeast Asian counterpoint to US/EU worker surveys. Limitation: online panel of employed internet users; market n=500 each gives +/-4-5% per-country margins.

title: AI Tracking Center: Tracking AI-Enabled Misinformation (AI Content Farm tracker)
authors: NewsGuard
verification: Tracker page read at origin 2026-11-05: 3,749 AI content-farm news/information sites identified and counting, spanning 16 languages (Arabic, Chinese, Czech, Dutch, English, French, German, Indonesian, Italian, Korean, Portuguese, Russian, Spanish, Tagalog, Thai, Turkish); last updated 23 June 2026. Inclusion requires all four criteria: substantial AI-produced content, publication without significant human oversight, presentation implying human journalism, and no clear AI disclosure. Recent AI-generated falsehoods cited include an AI-edited image of an Iranian missile inscribed with an 'Epstein Island' tribute and a fake Maduro arrest image (actually Saddam Hussein, 2003). Quarterly AI chatbot audits found leading tools repeat false claims on news topics roughly 28%-one-third of the time, including pro-Kremlin Pravda network claims repeated by major AI tools 33% of the time.
relevance: The reference supply-side measurement of AI-generated misinformation: NewsGuard's count of undisclosed AI content farms grew from roughly 1,200 sites in late 2024 to 2,089 (Oct 2025), 3,006 (Mar 2026) and 3,749 in sixteen languages by mid-2026, all monetised through programmatic advertising - documenting the industrialisation of untrustworthy AI news that feeds the 'faith in AI news' concern measured on the demand side by the Reuters Institute DNR 2025 already in the map. Its four-criteria methodology (AI-produced, no human oversight, masquerading as journalism, undisclosed) is a citable standard, and its chatbot audits showing major tools repeat false news claims 28-33% of the time quantify AI-as-misinformation-vector rather than just AI-as-content-farm. Limitation: a commercial vendor's tracker; site identification involves analyst judgment and the list is not an exhaustive census.
